lessons.title: Start here · Your Foundation 4.0 preparation route
lessons.summary: Understand the exam, choose a study route and preserve fresh mock papers.

blocks.text: This independent English study pack is aligned to CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, the errata revision for Foundation 4.0. It is not an official exam or accredited training course. Start with the six chapters, work through the examples, then use untimed learning sessions to understand mistakes. All examinable learning objectives are linked to lessons and practice.

blocks.title: Exam format
blocks.text: The full simulation has 40 multiple-choice questions worth one point each, 60 minutes and a pass mark of 26. Select-N questions require exactly the stated number and award no partial credit. Extended-time practice uses 75 minutes; eligibility for an actual language allowance is determined by your exam provider.

blocks.title: A practical route
blocks.text: First pass: read the lessons and solve self-checks before revealing their solutions. Second pass: work on technique calculations and review terminology. Third pass: take paper A under timed conditions, review every uncertain answer, and repeat with B, C and D on separate days. A 20-question short session is a practice exercise, not a full exam.

blocks.title: Fresh evidence
blocks.text: The four papers contain different questions. Taking the 75-minute version of a paper repeats its questions. Learning practice also exposes questions from this bank. Preserve at least three unopened full papers if you want to meet the default readiness rule: strictly above 90% on each of three full mocks with 100% fresh families. A simulated pass is separate from that recommendation.

blocks.title: Sources and authorship
blocks.text: ISTQB and the authors named in its syllabus own the official syllabus and exam-rule documents. This pack contains original explanations, examples and questions; it does not reproduce official sample exams. The pack source list links to official materials and the glossary. K1 means recall, K2 means understanding, and K3 means applying a technique.

blocks.title: Read beyond the objective list

Use these lessons as a guided study route, then read the corresponding syllabus sections and keyword lists. The numbered learning objectives identify additional K1, K2 and K3 expectations; they are not a complete list of examinable terms. Reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 0.5 (p. 11). For K3, practise deriving tests and performing calculations before viewing a solution.

blocks.title: Official reading
blocks.text: The pack sources link to the official syllabus, exam rules and exam blueprint tables. Lesson references and answer explanations give printed PDF page numbers so you can open the original document at the relevant section.

blocks.title: Use the expanded practice bank
blocks.text: Each syllabus-section lesson includes detailed concepts, a worked case, an exercise and a worked solution. Attempt the exercise before reading its solution, then explain the reasoning aloud. The bank includes 64 additional objective questions alongside the 160 questions in papers A-D. Learning and short sessions can draw from the full bank and expose paper questions. Preserve unopened papers for fresh full-mock evidence.

lessons.title: 1.1 · Testing and debugging
lessons.summary: Define test objectives, basis and oracles; distinguish verification, validation and debugging.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Testing evaluates work products and provides information for decisions. Activities include reviewing requirements, designing cases, executing software and reporting results. Objectives can include finding defects, assessing quality, reducing risk, checking contractual or regulatory requirements and building justified confidence. Verification asks whether specified requirements are met; validation asks whether the product meets stakeholder needs in its use context. Debugging investigates and removes the cause of a failure. A tester can reveal a failure without repairing its cause.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A checkout test reveals that a coupon increases the total. The tester records inputs, observed results and expected results. A developer locates a sign error, changes the code and runs component checks. The tester then confirms the fix and checks related discount behavior. Finding the failure was testing; diagnosing and repairing it was debugging.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Testing is broader than executing code, and a successful test does not prove that every defect has been removed.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A team reviews an unimplemented password requirement and finds ambiguity. Is this testing? Yes: static testing evaluates a work product without executing the software. Does the review debug code? No: no failure is being diagnosed and repaired.

blocks.title: Choose an objective before choosing a test
blocks.text: The objective identifies the information needed: whether a calculation follows a contractual rule, whether the product meets a user need, or whether the release carries unacceptable risk. The test basis is the source used to derive tests, such as requirements or a model. The object is the work product evaluated. A condition identifies an aspect to check; a case supplies preconditions, inputs and expected outcomes. An oracle helps determine those outcomes. A passing result supplies evidence under the selected conditions. It does not establish correctness of the entire product.

blocks.title: Worked case: delivery addresses
blocks.text: The specification requires a postal code. Checking rejection of an empty code supports verification. Observing customers in a country without postal codes can reveal that the specified design prevents legitimate orders, supporting validation. A product can satisfy its written rule and still fail its users. When a failure occurs, diagnosing and repairing its cause is debugging. Repeating the failure case after repair is confirmation testing.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A booking system implements a requirement to close appointments at 17:00, but evening patients need access until 20:00. State one verification question and one validation question. What activity describes repairing a wrong cutoff calculation?

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Verification asks whether booking stops at the specified boundary. Validation asks whether the cutoff supports actual patient and staff needs. Diagnosing and repairing the calculation is debugging; evaluating the repair is testing. Report the mismatch between specification and use context so stakeholders can agree a suitable rule.

lessons.title: 1.2 · Why testing matters
lessons.summary: Trace root causes, errors, defects and failures; distinguish process assurance from product evaluation.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Testing can prevent defects through early review and detect defects before users experience failures. Its evidence supports release decisions and reduces the cost of later rework. Quality assurance is concerned with improving processes; testing is a product-oriented quality-control activity. An error is a human mistake. A defect is a flaw in a work product. A failure is observed incorrect behavior when a defect is triggered. A root cause is an underlying reason that helps explain why the mistake or defect arose.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A rushed developer misreads an unclear fee rule (error), writes the wrong comparison (defect), and customers are charged incorrectly for one account class (failure). An absent requirement review may be a root cause. Repairing the comparison addresses this defect; improving requirement reviews may prevent similar defects.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A defect need not cause a failure on every execution. Testing and QA contribute to quality through different activities; testing does not guarantee quality by itself.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Would correcting the comparison alone eliminate the underlying process weakness? No. Would reviewing the fee requirement be useful before coding? Yes: it can expose ambiguity before it becomes an implementation defect.

blocks.title: Follow cause, mistake, flaw and observation
blocks.text: A root cause explains why a problem arose, such as missing domain training. A human error can introduce a defect into a requirement, design or program. A defect can cause a failure when relevant conditions trigger it. One defect can cause several failures; another can remain dormant. Testing supplies evidence about product quality. Quality assurance improves the processes used to create and evaluate products, including development processes. Fixing an immediate product problem and improving its originating process are different useful actions.

blocks.title: Worked case: payroll
blocks.text: An analyst misunderstands a regional tax exception because onboarding omitted it, writes an incorrect formula, and a developer implements that formula. A test reveals that an eligible employee receives too little pay. Missing onboarding is a candidate root cause, misunderstanding is the error, the faulty formula is a defect, and observed incorrect pay is a failure. Repair the formula and investigate whether related rules share the misunderstanding. Improve onboarding and review practices to reduce recurrence.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A team introduces a requirement-review checklist and executes refund scenarios on the next build. Which action primarily improves a process, and which evaluates the product? Why can one repaired failure leave other failures possible?

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Improving the review process is quality assurance; executing refund scenarios is testing, a quality-control activity. Another defect can remain, or a repair can adversely affect related behavior. Confirmation checks the reported fix; regression checks relevant existing behavior. Neither establishes the absence of defects.

lessons.title: 1.3 · Seven testing principles
lessons.summary: Apply the seven principles to changing risks, coverage choices and release arguments.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Remember seven ideas: tests can show defects but cannot establish their absence; exhaustive testing is generally infeasible; early testing saves resources; defects often cluster; tests lose effectiveness when repeatedly used without revision; testing depends on context; and a defect-free implementation can still fail to meet user needs. Use risk to choose where effort matters. Refresh tests when risks or behavior change, while retaining useful regression checks. Clustering is an observation that guides investigation, not a rule that untested areas are safe.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A mobile banking team discovers many failures in currency conversion and invests more testing there. It also checks critical login and transfer workflows. Repeating an unchanged currency suite for months stops finding new issues, so the team adds combinations suggested by recent changes and incidents.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Absence of observed failures is not proof of absence of defects. “Tests wear out” does not mean deleting the regression suite.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A product satisfies every written requirement but customers cannot complete their main task. Which principle explains this? The absence-of-defects fallacy: meeting a specification does not establish usefulness.

blocks.title: Use principles to justify scope
blocks.text: The seven principles explain why test results need context. Testing can reveal defects but cannot establish their absence. Exhaustiveness is infeasible for most realistic systems, making selection necessary. Early evaluation can reduce rework. Defects tend to cluster, making historical hotspots useful leads. Repeated checks can lose effectiveness against new defects, so refresh tests as behavior changes. Context determines a suitable approach. Finally, a correct implementation of a flawed specification can still fail stakeholder needs.

blocks.title: Worked case: new authentication risks
blocks.text: A dashboard has passed its established login suite for months. A new identity provider adds token expiry, redirects and revoked accounts. Retain useful regression checks and add cases for these risks. Investigate historical access-control hotspots early, but also check newly introduced exports. Clustering does not establish safety elsewhere. A disposable prototype and a safety-critical dashboard can require different rigor even when both have login screens.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A manager says: “The old suite passed, previous defects clustered in login, and the new reports meet their specifications. We can release.” Identify three missing considerations.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Repeated checks may miss new risks; clustering guides attention but does not establish safety in other areas; and satisfying specifications does not establish usefulness. Review changed scope, collect suitable coverage evidence, evaluate realistic stakeholder tasks and communicate residual risk before the decision.

lessons.title: 1.4 · Test activities, testware and roles
lessons.summary: Connect activities to testware and trace requirements through cases, results and defects.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Planning defines objectives, approach, resources and criteria. Monitoring compares progress with the plan; control adjusts actions. Analysis identifies what to test from the test basis. Design decides how to test and develops cases and coverage items. Implementation prepares procedures, suites, data and environments. Execution runs tests and records outcomes. Completion consolidates evidence, archives useful testware and captures lessons. Activities overlap and depend on risk, lifecycle, constraints and stakeholders. Testware includes plans, conditions, cases, procedures, data, logs and reports. Traceability links the basis, conditions, tests, results and defects. A test-management role coordinates the work; a testing role performs technical activities. One person may perform both.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Requirement R7 links to condition C3, cases T8 and T9, execution E2 and defect D4. When R7 changes, these links identify affected tests. A test log records observations; a completion report summarizes outcomes and unresolved risk for a release decision.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Analysis identifies conditions; design derives cases; implementation prepares executable testware. A job title does not uniquely determine a testing role.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A team prepares accounts and a reusable execution procedure. Which activity? Implementation. It then compares executed cases against the target and changes priorities. Which activities? Monitoring and control.

blocks.title: Trace activities to their outputs
blocks.text: Analysis derives conditions from the basis; design turns conditions into cases, coverage items, data requirements and expected results. Implementation prepares procedures, suites, environments and execution order. Execution records observations and anomalies. Monitoring assesses progress; control adjusts actions. Completion consolidates evidence and reusable testware at a milestone. Activities can overlap. Traceability connects basis, conditions, cases, results and defects, supporting both coverage and change-impact analysis. A test-management role coordinates work; a testing role performs technical analysis and evaluation.

blocks.title: Worked case: cancellation trace
blocks.text: Requirement R17 permits cancellation until dispatch. Condition C8 concerns the order state; TC31 and TC32 cover Packed and Dispatched. Run RUN9 records pass and fail; D4 links to TC32. When R17 changes to allow cancellation until carrier collection, these links identify affected cases. Results from the old rule remain evidence about the earlier configuration. Management arranges resources; the testing role updates the conditions and expected outcomes.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A report gives a 90% pass rate with no links to requirements or risks. Identify two relationships needed to assess a changed payment feature.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Link requirements or risks to conditions and cases to show planned scope. Link cases to versioned executions and defects to show achieved evidence. A high pass rate can reflect repeated low-risk checks while important changed behavior remains untested. Preserve the product and basis revisions behind the results.

lessons.title: 1.5 · Skills, teamwork and independence
lessons.summary: Use complementary skills, factual communication and suitable independence in a whole team.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Useful tester skills include analytical thinking, curiosity, care, communication, domain understanding and technical knowledge. Communicate observable facts without blaming people. In a whole-team approach, quality is a shared responsibility and people contribute complementary skills; testers help others develop testing competence. Independence can reveal assumptions that authors share, but excessive separation can weaken collaboration, create bottlenecks or shift perceived ownership of quality away from developers. Choose a degree of independence appropriate to the risk and context.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A tester discusses a confusing delivery rule with a business specialist and developer. The specialist clarifies user needs, the tester proposes examples, and the developer explains technical constraints. A separately assigned reviewer later challenges an assumption all three missed.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Independence is not a reason to isolate testers. A whole-team approach does not remove specialist skills or make everyone equally capable of every task.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Rewrite “Your code is broken” as useful feedback. Example: “For account type X on build 18, the displayed fee is 12; the agreed example expects 10. These steps reproduce it.”

blocks.title: Combine perspectives and communicate facts
blocks.text: Analytical thinking divides problems into conditions; curiosity suggests overlooked situations; domain and technical knowledge improve test plausibility. Report observations, expectations, conditions and consequences rather than personal blame. Independence ranges from author checks through peers, another team and an external organization. Different backgrounds can challenge shared assumptions, but separation can create communication gaps and reduce shared ownership. Choose independence according to risk while maintaining access to expertise. Whole-team quality responsibility uses complementary skills rather than making every person perform every specialist task.

blocks.title: Worked case: transport fares
blocks.text: A developer checks calculation units, an independent tester checks transfers, and a station supervisor evaluates passenger journeys. The developer understands the fare cache, the supervisor knows two stations share an entrance, and the tester challenges assumptions about stale fares after a tariff change. Sharing these observations combines perspectives. None should be used as a reason to remove another participant’s quality responsibility.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Rewrite “The developer does not understand discounts” when the actual observation is that 15% off a 200-unit basket produces 185 rather than 170. Name a useful independent perspective.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Report the build, inputs and rule: “Applying 15% off a 200-unit basket produces 185; the agreed calculation gives 170. Reproduction steps are attached.” A business representative can clarify whether discount is applied before tax; a peer can challenge calculation assumptions. This makes the finding actionable without unsupported personal claims.

lessons.title: 2.1 · Testing across development lifecycles
lessons.summary: Adapt feedback to the lifecycle, compare test-first approaches and evaluate retrospective improvements.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Sequential lifecycles often connect planned test levels to corresponding development activities. Iterative and incremental development needs testing of new increments and regression of existing behavior. Across lifecycles, involve testers early, associate testing with development work, review work products when available and plan test levels with appropriate objectives. TDD uses component tests before implementation; ATDD starts from agreed acceptance examples; BDD expresses expected behavior in business-readable scenarios. DevOps encourages collaboration, automation and rapid feedback, while requiring reliable environments and maintained pipelines. Shift left moves suitable testing earlier; it complements testing later in delivery. Retrospectives examine outcomes and agree improvements whose effects should be checked.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: During refinement, three roles agree an acceptance example. A developer writes a failing check, implements behavior and refactors after it passes. A delivery pipeline runs checks on commits and deploys to a controlled environment. A retrospective discovers flaky test data and assigns an owner to fix it.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Shift left does not eliminate system or acceptance testing. Automated pipelines are useful only when their feedback is trustworthy.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: An action item says “improve testing.” Make it actionable. Example: “By next iteration, stabilize the five flaky checkout cases and compare rerun frequency before and after.”

blocks.title: Build feedback into the lifecycle
blocks.text: Sequential development can use reviews and case design before executable code exists. Incremental development repeatedly needs new-feature and regression evidence. Across lifecycles, involve testers early, review available drafts, give levels distinct objectives, and start analysis during corresponding development activities. TDD uses a test, implementation and refactoring loop. ATDD starts with jointly agreed acceptance examples. BDD expresses behavior in stakeholder-readable scenarios. DevOps connects development, testing and operations with maintained pipelines and fast feedback. Shift left complements later evaluation.

blocks.title: Worked case: subscription upgrade
blocks.text: Business staff and testers clarify upgrade and cancellation examples. Developers write component checks for prorated charges before implementation. Continuous integration runs checks and static analysis; a representative environment supports integration and performance evaluation. A tester explores interrupted upgrades. An iteration review identifies stale price fixtures as a blocker, so the team versions fixtures and assigns ownership of provisioning.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A retrospective repeatedly identifies stale environment data. Propose an improvement, an owner and a measure that would show whether it helped.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Version and verify the fixture during provisioning, assign ownership and an adoption date, and track blocked hours or fixture mismatches in subsequent iterations. Evaluating the change completes the improvement loop. Recording the complaint without action and follow-up supplies little evidence of improvement.

lessons.title: 2.2 · Test levels, types and change checks
lessons.summary: Distinguish levels, types and purposes using component, system and external-bank checks.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Component testing checks individual components; component integration checks interactions among components; system testing checks the whole system; system integration checks interactions with other systems or services; acceptance testing assesses readiness and stakeholder needs. Test levels differ in objects, objectives, basis, responsibilities and typical defects. Functional testing examines what a system does; non-functional testing examines qualities such as performance or usability. Black-box testing uses behavior without relying on internal structure; white-box testing derives checks from structure. Confirmation testing checks whether a specific defect was fixed. Regression testing checks whether a change adversely affected existing behavior.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: After repairing tax rounding, rerunning the failing rounding case is confirmation. Checking discounts, invoices and refunds is regression. Measuring response time under load is non-functional testing. Checking exchange of messages with a payment gateway is system integration.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A test level is not a test type. The same test type can be applied at multiple levels, and regression can follow changes outside source code.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A user representative checks whether a payroll product supports the agreed month-end workflow. Which level is the primary focus? Acceptance. If an API contract with a bank is checked instead, system integration is the focus.

blocks.title: Distinguish level, type and purpose
blocks.text: A level identifies the object’s scope: component, component integration, system, system integration or acceptance. A type identifies a quality or perspective, such as functional behavior, performance or internal structure. Several types can occur at several levels. Component integration concerns interactions inside the system; system integration concerns external-system interfaces. Acceptance evaluates readiness and stakeholder needs. Confirmation checks a repaired defect; regression checks adverse effects of a change. Purpose and level can apply together to the same check.

blocks.title: Worked case: shop architecture
blocks.text: Check a tax function in isolation at component level, cart/tax interaction at component integration, an assembled order journey at system, and exchange with the external bank at system integration. Finance staff evaluating settlement readiness supports acceptance. Timing checks can be applied at several of these levels; performance focus alone does not establish level.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: After fixing duplicate charging, the team repeats the original double-click case, checks ordinary purchases and refunds, and evaluates the external bank interface. Identify the first two purposes and the interface check’s level.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: The original failure case supplies confirmation evidence. Purchases and refunds supply regression evidence. The external bank interaction is system integration. An interface check may also serve confirmation or regression, depending on why it was selected.

lessons.title: 2.3 · Maintenance testing
lessons.summary: Analyze operational changes, migrations and retirement to choose maintenance scope.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Maintenance testing evaluates changes to operational software and the effects on existing behavior. Triggers include modifications, migrations and retirement. A defect fix, operating-system update, infrastructure migration or changed configuration can create risk even when application code is untouched. Impact analysis identifies affected components, interfaces, data and stakeholders, then helps select confirmation and regression scope. Scope depends on change size, system size and risk.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A business moves its reporting database to a new platform. Tests check migrated data, queries, permissions, integrations and critical existing reports. Before retiring the old service, the team checks archival access and retention obligations.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Maintenance testing is not restricted to bug fixes. A seemingly small platform change may affect many consumers.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: What should guide regression selection after a library upgrade? Impact analysis and risk, including dependencies and interfaces; the number of changed application lines is insufficient.

blocks.title: Analyze operational change before selecting scope
blocks.text: Maintenance changes include enhancements, repairs, configuration updates, platform changes, migration and retirement. Identify affected dependencies, data, interfaces, users and quality characteristics. Change size, system size and risk influence scope. A small setting can affect many services, while unchanged source can run differently on a new platform. Retirement may require checks of archival access, retention and recovery. Confirmation and risk-based regression remain relevant after repairs.

blocks.title: Worked case: archive migration
blocks.text: A records service moves to another storage provider. Contents remain the same, but permissions, object names, timeouts and links can differ. Compare representative records, check permitted and prohibited access, interrupt retrieval and verify retention behavior. Identify applications consuming the links. Keep evidence of the migration configuration and confirm any repaired lookup defect before regression of search and export.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A booking service upgrades its database driver with no application-source changes. Give three impact questions and explain why a login check is insufficient.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Ask about transaction semantics, numeric/date conversion and shared consumers of the driver. Check relevant commits, rollbacks, conversions and interfaces according to risk. Login shows limited availability evidence; it does not exercise the likely consequences of the update.

lessons.title: 3.1 · Static testing
lessons.summary: Select review, static analysis and execution according to the evidence each can provide.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Static testing examines work products without executing the software under test. Reviews can examine requirements, user stories, designs, source code, test cases, contracts and user documentation. Static analysis tools can inspect suitably structured artifacts for issues such as unreachable code, inconsistent interfaces or coding-rule violations. Early static testing finds defects directly and can prevent expensive later rework. Dynamic testing executes software and reveals failures. Both provide complementary evidence: static review can find missing or contradictory requirements, while dynamic testing can assess behavior and runtime qualities.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A requirement says “respond quickly.” A review exposes missing measurable acceptance criteria before code exists. Static analysis identifies an unused variable in source. A load test later measures whether the implemented service meets the agreed response-time target.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Static testing finds defects directly; dynamic testing observes failures that may lead to defect investigation. Static testing does not require executable code.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Can a test plan be statically tested? Yes: a review can reveal missing scope, inconsistent criteria or invalid assumptions. Can response time under actual load be established by that review? No: runtime evidence is needed.

blocks.title: Match a method to the evidence needed
blocks.text: Review finds omissions, ambiguity and contradictions directly in work products. Static analysis uses formal structure to detect suspicious patterns or rule violations; findings may need human interpretation. Dynamic testing executes the object and can assess behavior, time and resource consumption. Reviewing an unimplemented requirement is possible; measuring runtime latency requires execution. Finding a defect directly differs from observing a failure and investigating its cause. Combine methods because their strengths address different problems.

blocks.title: Worked case: document downloads
blocks.text: A review finds conflicting download limits in a requirement. Static analysis flags unreachable error handling. A dynamic check reveals a timeout on a slow connection. The first finding can prevent implementation of an incorrect rule; the timeout needs runtime evidence. Addressing one does not remove the need to investigate the others.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Choose evaluation methods for a missing API-contract field, a coding-standard violation and excessive latency.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Review the contract for omissions; use suitable static analysis or code review for coding rules; execute representative performance checks for latency. Comparing actual API responses with the contract can supplement the review. Explain what each method establishes and preserve its evidence.

lessons.title: 3.2 · Feedback and review process
lessons.summary: Prepare useful reviews, assign responsibilities and follow inspection findings through repair.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Early and frequent stakeholder feedback helps align understanding and discover changes before they become costly. A review typically involves planning, initiation, individual review, communication and analysis, then fixing and reporting. The author creates and updates the work product. Reviewers identify anomalies. A moderator facilitates effective meetings. A scribe records findings and decisions. A review leader coordinates the review; management supplies resources. Informal reviews have little prescribed process; walkthroughs are usually author-led; technical reviews involve qualified peers and aim at evaluation or consensus; inspections use the most formal process with defined roles and collected information. Clear objectives, suitable participants, small manageable work products, preparation and a constructive culture support success.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: For a payment specification, reviewers first inspect individually using a checklist. The moderator keeps the meeting focused on anomalies. The author clarifies findings, the scribe records decisions, and unresolved issues are tracked after the meeting.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Roles describe responsibilities, not necessarily separate people. A review should evaluate the work product rather than the author’s performance.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which activity comes before discussing findings in a formal review? Individual review. Which role writes down agreed findings during the meeting? The scribe.

blocks.title: Prepare, examine, analyze and follow up
blocks.text: Planning sets scope, objectives, roles and criteria. Initiation makes the work product and process available. Individual review identifies candidate anomalies. Communication and analysis agree findings and actions; fixing and reporting follow up. The author updates work, reviewers examine it, the moderator facilitates, the scribe records findings, the leader coordinates, and management supports resources. Walkthroughs are author-led; technical reviews use qualified peers; inspections are the most formal. An inspection’s author must not act as review leader or scribe.

blocks.title: Worked case: focused inspection
blocks.text: Inspect a manageable security requirement set with defined criteria and trained participants. Allocate preparation time. Reviewers bring findings; the moderator supports constructive discussion; the scribe records evidence and actions. Follow repairs and collect information for process improvement. Avoid treating defect counts as personal performance measures: that can discourage useful disclosure.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A manager schedules 200 pages with no preparation and plans to rank authors by defect counts. Propose three improvements.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Split material into manageable portions, allow preparation, and define objectives about the work product rather than ranking people. Provide suitable roles, training and support. Follow up on repairs and report outcomes against criteria. Large scope and personal criticism undermine concentration and constructive participation.

lessons.title: 4.1 · Choosing test techniques
lessons.summary: Identify specification, structure and experience as complementary bases for deriving cases.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Black-box techniques derive tests from specified behavior and do not require knowledge of implementation. White-box techniques derive tests from internal structure. Experience-based techniques draw on knowledge of past failures, domain risks and tester judgment. Techniques identify coverage items and help create a defensible selection of cases. They can be combined: requirements tell you what users need, structure reveals unexercised paths, and experience suggests likely problems.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A fee rule is tested with partitions of customer types (black-box). The team checks unexecuted decision outcomes (white-box). A tester adds a locale case after recalling a previous decimal-separator defect (experience-based).

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Black-box does not mean informal. Knowing the source code does not prevent you from deriving a test from a requirement.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A case is selected because a decision outcome has never run. What is the basis? Structure, so this is white-box. A case selected because a business rule distinguishes two account classes is black-box.

blocks.title: Classify cases by their derivation
blocks.text: Black-box cases arise from specified behavior even if the tester knows the code. White-box cases arise from internal structure even if they assert visible outputs. Experience-based cases arise from knowledge of likely faults and past failures. Each method identifies coverage items that guide selection. State what the denominator means before presenting a percentage. Methods can complement each other; reaching code alone may not reveal required behavior absent from that code.

blocks.title: Worked case: export evidence
blocks.text: Specified formats produce partitions for CSV, JSON and unsupported types. Structural analysis identifies streaming and buffered branches. Previous incidents suggest interrupted downloads and embedded delimiters. These are black-box, white-box and experience-based derivations respectively. Missing JSON implementation might escape complete statement coverage while specification-derived cases expose it.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Classify inputs chosen to reach internal decision outcomes, representatives of contract-defined customer classes, and timestamp rollover cases motivated by a past incident.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Internal decisions give a white-box basis, customer classes a black-box basis, and the remembered incident an experience-based basis. All may execute the application; execution does not change the source used to derive the cases.

lessons.title: 4.2 · Black-box techniques in practice
lessons.summary: Derive partitions, full boundary coverage, decision rules and state-transition paths.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Equivalence partitioning divides a data domain into groups expected to be processed similarly; test each relevant valid and invalid partition. Boundary value analysis focuses on edges of ordered partitions. Two-value BVA uses each boundary and its closest value in the adjacent partition; three-value BVA exercises each identified boundary value and both of its immediate neighbors. For full coverage across a partition edge, consider the boundary values on both sides of the edge. Decision tables relate condition combinations to actions: list conditions, enumerate feasible combinations, specify actions and derive cases for rules. Merge rules only when differences cannot affect actions. State transition testing models states, events and resulting states. State coverage, valid-transition coverage and all-transition coverage measure different items; tests for invalid transitions check rejected behavior without masking defects by chaining invalid events.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: An integer quantity is accepted from 3 to 7. EP partitions are below 3, 3–7 and above 7; representatives 2, 5 and 8 cover them. Two-value BVA uses 2,3,7,8; full three-value BVA across both partition edges uses 1,2,3,4,6,7,8,9. Two independent Boolean conditions yield four combinations before excluding infeasible rules. A door model has Closed → Open on unlock and Open → Closed on lock; visiting both states need not exercise every event.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Partition coverage is not coverage of every combination of partitions. Boundaries apply to ordered partitions. Reaching every state does not guarantee traversing every transition.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: For a valid range of 1–5 inclusive integers, give full three-value BVA across both partition edges, assuming negative integers are possible inputs. Solution: -1,0,1,2,4,5,6,7. For a rule requiring both consent and an active account, which combination permits access? Both true; the other three combinations deny access.

blocks.title: Derive cases from explicit coverage items
blocks.text: EP needs nonempty, nonoverlapping partitions expected to be processed similarly, including invalid partitions. Each Choice across multiple inputs covers each partition from each set, not all combinations. BVA needs ordered partitions and a value step. Two-value coverage reaches boundaries across partition edges. Full three-value coverage includes both immediate neighbors of each boundary, including boundaries on both sides of an edge. Decision tables count feasible rules. State coverage, valid-transition coverage and all-transition coverage count different items; visiting all states can miss transitions.

blocks.title: Worked case: four techniques
blocks.text:
EP: integer quantity is accepted from 3 to 8. Values 2, 5, 9 cover below, within and above range.
BVA: two-value coverage uses 2, 3, 8, 9. Full three-value coverage uses 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10 after removing duplicates.
Decision table: a voucher requires registered AND qualifying purchase. TT, TF, FT, FF are four feasible rules; issue for TT, decline for the others.
States: Draft --submit--> Pending --approve--> Approved; Pending --reject--> Draft. Submit then approve visits all states but misses rejection.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: An integer score is valid from 20 through 24. Derive full two-value and three-value coverage across both edges. Four of six feasible decision rules have been exercised: calculate coverage. Give a path exercising all three transitions in the Draft/Pending/Approved model.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Two-value: 19, 20, 24, 25. Three-value: 18, 19, 20, 21, 23, 24, 25, 26. The lower boundaries are 19 and 20, the upper 24 and 25; add both neighbors of each, then deduplicate. Decision coverage is 4/6, about 66.7%. Submit, reject, submit, approve covers all valid transitions. Exercise invalid events separately from clear starting states to avoid defect masking.

lessons.title: 4.3 · White-box coverage
lessons.summary: Calculate statement and branch coverage and explain what structural percentages leave unresolved.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Statement coverage is executed executable statements divided by total executable statements. Branch coverage is executed control-flow branches divided by total branches. Use the model given in the question to identify branches; conditional decisions generally have both true and false outcomes. Full branch coverage implies full statement coverage for the modeled executable structure, but full statement coverage can miss a branch. Structural coverage can expose untested implementation and support useful checks, but it cannot reveal behavior that was never implemented merely by reaching code.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Pseudocode: if member then applyDiscount; printTotal. A member test executes both statements, achieving full statement coverage, but misses the false outcome of the decision. Adding a non-member test exercises that branch. If four of five executable statements run, statement coverage is 4/5 × 100 = 80%.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Do not infer branch coverage from a statement percentage. Even 100% coverage does not establish correctness or complete requirements coverage.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A model has eight branches; six run. Coverage is 6/8 × 100 = 75%. What additional evidence is needed before calling the product correct? Assertions against expected behavior, requirements and risk-based tests beyond structural reachability.

blocks.title: Count implementation items before interpreting coverage
blocks.text: Statements are executable items, not automatically comments or declarations. Branch items are control-flow transfers, including unconditional branches when present in the specified model. Simplified questions may explicitly count true/false decision outcomes. Full branch coverage implies full statement coverage; the reverse is false. Neither metric establishes defect removal, requirements completeness or every possible path. Structural evidence needs meaningful checks of the executed behavior and complementary evidence from the specification.

blocks.title: Worked case: an optional surcharge
blocks.text: Use this simplified model with four executable statements: total = base; if express then total = total + 5; receipt = total; save(receipt). Count the surcharge assignment as the second statement and the two decision outcomes as branch items. An express case executes all four statements but only one decision outcome: 100% statement coverage and 50% branch coverage in this model. A non-express case reaches the other outcome. A missing tax requirement can still escape these checks.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A stated model has ten executable statements and six branch items. Eight statements and four branches execute. Calculate both percentages. Does this establish that 80% of requirements are satisfied?

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Statement coverage is 8/10=80%; branch coverage is 4/6, about 66.7%. Requirements have a different denominator and need traceability. Reached code can contain defects, so interpret the result with assertions, outcomes and specification-derived evidence.

lessons.title: 4.4 · Experience-based techniques
lessons.summary: Turn experience into fault attacks, focused exploratory charters and maintained checklists.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Error guessing uses knowledge of typical mistakes and previous defects to propose tests. Exploratory testing combines learning, design and execution as the tester responds to observations; it is often organized into time-boxed sessions with charters, notes and debriefs. Checklist-based testing uses a maintained list of conditions to guide consistent checking while allowing judgment in the detailed cases. All three can complement systematic techniques, particularly where specifications are incomplete. Their effectiveness depends on relevant expertise and on documenting enough evidence to communicate results.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A tester guesses that a copied discount rule might mishandle a zero amount. In an exploratory session with a “recover after payment interruption” charter, observations guide the next checks. A release checklist reminds the team to verify keyboard access, validation messages and recovery from network loss.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Exploratory testing is not unrecorded random clicking. A checklist guides coverage but is not automatically a detailed executable procedure.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which technique best fits a 45-minute investigation where each result informs the next experiment? Exploratory testing. How can the session remain accountable? Use a charter, record observations and summarize coverage and findings.

blocks.title: Give experience a mission and preserve evidence
blocks.text: Error guessing turns knowledge of likely faults into checks, such as missing inputs, incorrect operators and interface mismatches. Fault attacks organize possible faults into a list and derive revealing tests. Exploratory testing combines learning, design and execution; observations guide the next check. A charter defines a mission, a timebox bounds the session, and notes and debrief preserve useful information. Checklists supply reusable conditions while leaving detailed cases to judgment. Update them when risks and knowledge change.

blocks.title: Worked case: interrupted checkout
blocks.text: Charter: investigate resuming checkout after network interruption. In a 30-minute session, vary interruption around address save, authorization and confirmation. Record build, account, inputs, observations and unexplored questions. If a retry duplicates authorization, investigate related timing. Prior incidents suggest stale sessions; a checklist reminds the tester to check persistence and messages. The session has a purpose while adapting to discoveries.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Improve the note “clicked around checkout; seemed fine.” Explain what to do if retry creates a second authorization.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Add charter, build/environment, explored conditions and inputs, results, supporting evidence and unresolved scope. Investigate reproduction and related retry conditions, then report the observed behavior. Exploratory work adapts while preserving enough evidence for follow-up; random click count does not measure its value.

lessons.title: 4.5 · Collaborative acceptance testing
lessons.summary: Clarify acceptance rules collaboratively and derive positive, negative and boundary examples.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: User stories describe a user, a need and its value. The card is a starting point for conversation; confirmation is captured in acceptance criteria. Business representatives, developers and testers develop a shared understanding through examples. Acceptance criteria may be scenario-oriented, such as Given/When/Then, or rule-oriented, such as a checklist of constraints. Criteria define what must be met and should support unambiguous evaluation. ATDD derives acceptance tests collaboratively before implementation; include positive, negative and relevant non-functional cases and resolve inconsistent examples early.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Story: “As a subscriber, I want to pause renewals so I can avoid unwanted charges.” Criterion: Given an active subscription, when the user pauses before the renewal cutoff, then no renewal charge is made. Tests should cover a timely pause, a request after cutoff, an already paused account and resumption according to agreed rules.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A story is not complete simply because its card exists. Acceptance criteria describe behavior; they need not prescribe implementation details.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Criterion: purchases of at least 50 qualify for free delivery. An ATDD case uses a total of 50 and expects zero delivery charge; a negative case uses 49.99 and expects the specified paid-delivery amount. Agree that amount before automating the case.

blocks.title: Resolve examples before implementing rules
blocks.text: A story identifies who needs a capability, what is needed and why. The card starts a conversation; confirmation captures acceptance criteria. Developers, testers and business representatives contribute complementary perspectives. Scenario-oriented criteria describe a concrete situation and outcome; rule-oriented criteria list constraints. ATDD derives acceptance tests before implementation, including positive, negative and relevant quality cases. Conflicting examples expose a need for clarification rather than a reason to choose an arbitrary implementation.

blocks.title: Worked case: parcel locker
blocks.text: A code must match the parcel, be unexpired and belong to an uncollected parcel. Agree a positive example and expect the assigned door to open. Isolate negative cases for a wrong code, expiry, and reuse after collection. Clarify the expiry boundary: strictly before 18:00 implies rejection at 18:00. Agree time precision and timezone. If opening speed matters, define an observable response-time criterion rather than “quickly.”

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A ticket is refundable when unused and requested at least 48 hours before departure. Give an accepted case, two rejected cases isolating different rules, and a boundary question.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Accept unused/60 hours. Reject used/60 hours to isolate usage and unused/47 hours to isolate time. Ask how exactly 48 hours is interpreted and which timestamps, timezone and precision apply. “At least” suggests inclusion, but examples should confirm shared understanding before implementation.

lessons.title: 5.1 · Planning, estimates and priorities
lessons.summary: Connect plans and criteria with effort estimates, coverage priorities, pyramids and quadrants.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: A test plan states objectives, scope, approach, resources, schedule, responsibilities and criteria. Testers contribute to release and iteration planning by identifying risks, testability concerns and effort. Entry criteria describe conditions for starting an activity; exit criteria describe conditions for completion. Estimate effort from relevant historical ratios, extrapolation, expert consensus or three-point estimates. In the three-point formula used here, E = (optimistic + 4 × most likely + pessimistic) / 6. State assumptions and uncertainty. Prioritize by risk, coverage or requirements importance, then account for dependencies and resources. A test pyramid favors many small fast checks and fewer broad slower checks. Testing quadrants organize technology/business focus and support/critiquing purpose: Q1 component checks, Q2 business-facing examples supporting work, Q3 business-facing evaluation, Q4 technology-facing quality evaluation. A related three-point uncertainty estimate is SD=(pessimistic−optimistic)/6; for O=6 and P=18 days, SD=2 days. This is distinct from expected effort.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: For O=4, M=7 and P=16 hours, E=(4+28+16)/6=8 hours. If execution of a high-risk payment test requires account setup, setup must run first. A coverage-based order starts with the case covering the most items; additional-coverage ordering then chooses cases covering the most still-uncovered items.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: An estimate is not a commitment without uncertainty. Highest priority does not override a prerequisite. Quadrants are not chronological phases or fixed test levels.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Three teams report 10, 14 and 18 hours. Can their arithmetic mean alone remove uncertainty? No: discuss assumptions. If T1 covers A,B,C; T2 covers B,C; T3 covers D,E, additional-coverage order is T1,T3,T2.

blocks.title: Connect planning, criteria and uncertainty
blocks.text: A plan communicates scope, objectives, basis, risks, approach, responsibilities, data, environments, budget and schedule. Release planning spans iterations; iteration planning refines immediate tasks. Entry criteria identify prerequisites; exit criteria identify completion expectations. Deadline expiry does not turn unmet criteria into satisfied criteria: report the gap and seek an informed decision. Estimates can use historical ratios, extrapolation, expert consensus or three points. State assumptions. The pyramid suggests many fast isolated checks and fewer broad checks; quadrants classify focus and purpose rather than sequence.

blocks.title: Worked case: estimates and prioritization
blocks.text:
A historical test/development ratio of 0.4 with 50 developer-days suggests 20 tester-days if context is comparable. With O=4, M=7, P=16 days, E=(4+4x7+16)/6=8 days and SD=(16-4)/6=2 days.
T1 covers A,B,C; T2 A,B; T3 D,E. Total coverage places T1 first. After T1, additional coverage prefers T3 because it adds two items while T2 adds none. Dependencies can constrain the execution order.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Calculate E and SD for O=3, M=6, P=15 days. T2 covers Q,R,S and is selected; T1 covers P,Q and T3 T,U. Which adds more? Classify component checks, guiding acceptance examples, user exploration and load evaluation into quadrants.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: E=(3+24+15)/6=7 days; SD=(15-3)/6=2 days. T1 adds P; T3 adds T,U, so prefer T3 for additional coverage. Component support is Q1; business examples guiding development Q2; user-focused critique Q3; technology-focused load critique Q4. These models support decisions but do not prescribe a single fixed execution sequence.

lessons.title: 5.2 · Risk management
lessons.summary: Assess project and product risks, choose mitigation and monitor remaining exposure.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: A risk is an uncertain event with possible adverse consequences. Risk level combines likelihood and impact, often by multiplication of agreed scales. Project risks threaten delivery, such as staff loss or unavailable environments. Product risks threaten product quality, such as wrong payments or insecure access. Product risk analysis identifies and assesses risks; it guides scope, effort, techniques, coverage and priority. Possible responses include mitigation, acceptance, transfer and contingency planning. Testing reduces uncertainty and can reduce the probability of delivering defects, but residual risk remains and must be communicated.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Risk A has likelihood 2 and impact 5, level 10; risk B has likelihood 4 and impact 2, level 8. Under that model A ranks higher. Delayed environment delivery is a project risk; incorrect transaction totals are a product risk. More thorough checks may be allocated to totals because financial consequences are severe.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Risk likelihood is not impact. Multiplying ordinal ratings is a prioritization convention, not a precise probability of loss. A passing suite does not erase residual risk.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A release contains an untested authentication change. What should a status report include? The affected risk, missing evidence, consequences and proposed actions so the decision-maker can make an informed acceptance or mitigation decision.

blocks.title: Use risk assessment to choose actions
blocks.text: Identification lists adverse events; assessment considers likelihood, impact and priority. Project risks threaten schedule, resources or scope; product risks threaten delivered quality. Quantitative levels can multiply likelihood and impact; qualitative matrices use agreed categories. Ordinal scores are not calibrated probabilities. Risk-based testing uses the analysis to select levels, types, techniques, coverage and effort. Mitigation implements actions; monitoring checks their effectiveness and emerging exposure. Acceptance, transfer and contingency planning are other responses.

blocks.title: Worked case: invoice priorities
blocks.text: On a 1-5 scale, incorrect tax has likelihood 3 and impact 5, score 15; cosmetic alignment has 4 and 1, score 4. Prioritize tax-rule review, boundaries, combinations and regression. Separately, an unavailable test service threatens schedule: arrange controlled substitution and later real-interface evidence. Report remaining financial risk if needed data cannot be tested. These scores support comparison, not exact forecasts of failure rates.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Authorization checks and tests mitigate invoice-access risk. What evidence should be monitored, and why is a falling overall defect count insufficient?

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Monitor relevant role/ownership coverage, denied-access outcomes, unresolved findings and new paths introduced by changes. Reassess the risk using this evidence. A falling count can reflect less testing or fewer cosmetic findings; it does not establish effective mitigation of unauthorized access.

lessons.title: 5.3 · Monitoring, control and communication
lessons.summary: Interpret metric denominators and report scope, blockers and consequences for decisions.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Monitor progress, coverage, defects, effort, cost and quality signals against the plan. Metrics need context: counts of executed tests say little without scope, results and risk. Control actions may change priorities, resources, schedule or scope in response to evidence. Progress reports support ongoing decisions; completion reports summarize achieved objectives, results, deviations and unresolved risks at a milestone. Tailor detail and format to the audience. Developers may need reproducible findings; managers need consequences and decisions; distributed teams benefit from clear written records in addition to discussion.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A report says 80 of 100 tests ran, with 12 failures concentrated in checkout and 20 security cases blocked by an environment issue. A manager sees release exposure, while engineers receive failure details. A control action restores the environment and brings high-risk security checks forward.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A high pass percentage can conceal missing high-risk coverage. Reports should distinguish what was tested from what remains unknown.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: The plan expects 90 executions, but 45 are complete. Identifying the deviation is monitoring; deciding to reallocate engineers is control. For a release meeting, include residual risk and decision requests rather than only raw logs.

blocks.title: Give metrics a denominator and a decision
blocks.text: Monitoring gathers progress, quality, defect, coverage, cost and risk evidence. Control changes priorities, resources, scope or schedule in response. Completion consolidates evidence and reusable testware at milestones. Progress reports support ongoing control; completion reports summarize achieved objectives, deviations and remaining issues. Tailor detail to the audience. Record build and scope, distinguish failed, blocked and unexecuted cases, and state the denominator. A developer needs reproduction evidence; a sponsor needs release implications.

blocks.title: Worked case: interpret pass rate
blocks.text: Of 120 planned cases, 80 passed, 10 failed, 20 are blocked and 10 unexecuted. Executed-case pass rate is 80/90, about 88.9%; planned-case pass percentage is 80/120, about 66.7%; execution progress is 90/120=75%. None establishes risk coverage. If blocked cases concern settlements, restore that environment or communicate the gap rather than simply running more already-covered checks.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A release has completed 95% of cases, but the remaining 5% concerns deletion and retention of personal data. Outline a useful stakeholder update.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: State the build and completed scope, the untested scenarios and consequences, the blocker, owner and expected resolution. Identify unmet exit criteria and residual risk. Request a decision about further testing or an explicit exception. A percentage without the high-impact gap can mislead stakeholders.

lessons.title: 5.4 · Configuration management
lessons.summary: Preserve versioned configurations and baselines so results remain reproducible.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Configuration management identifies, versions, controls and relates items needed for reproducible testing. Relevant items include requirements, builds, tests, data, environment configuration and results. A baseline is an agreed set of versions that can be referenced consistently. Traceability plus version control helps determine which result applies to which product and test basis. Controlled changes make impact analysis and investigation more reliable.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A test result links application build 82, requirement revision 4, test suite 11 and data set 6. When a failure cannot be reproduced on build 83, the team can restore the original baseline and compare the change.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A test result detached from its build and environment may be misleading even if the test passed. Versioning source code alone does not control all test dependencies.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which information makes a data-dependent failure reproducible? The product version, procedure, environment and data version, as well as actual and expected results. “It failed last week” is insufficient.

blocks.title: Preserve the configuration behind observations
blocks.text: Configuration management identifies and controls basis, build, cases, data, environment settings, tools and results. A baseline is an agreed configuration that can be referenced consistently. Traceability relates items; versions distinguish revisions. A result without its build and data revision may become uninterpretable after a change. Preserve controlled changes and status information to support reproduction, impact analysis and understanding which configurations have actually been evaluated.

blocks.title: Worked case: different currency totals
blocks.text: One tester uses B18 with fixture D7 and locale L2; another uses B19 with D8 and L2. Record configurations, compare changes and repeat under a shared baseline. The difference could be implementation or data. Retain earlier results as evidence of their original configuration rather than overwriting them with outcomes from the new build.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A refund screenshot says “latest build, normal data.” Name four details that support reproduction and explain how to record a run after fixture changes.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Record exact build, case revision, fixture revision and relevant environment settings such as partner-service configuration. Link the applicable requirement revision. Preserve the earlier evidence and give the new run its own configuration. Calling both “latest” obscures the relationship between changes and outcomes.

lessons.title: 5.5 · Writing actionable defect reports
lessons.summary: Write actionable defect reports with reproduction evidence, impact and assessed urgency.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: A defect report should let its audience understand impact, reproduce the observation and assess next actions. Include a clear title, unique reference, reporter and date, affected product and environment, preconditions, reproducible steps, actual and expected results, supporting evidence, severity, priority and status as appropriate. Severity describes impact; priority describes urgency. Keep observations distinct from hypotheses about the cause. A reported anomaly may require investigation before it is confirmed as a defect.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Title: “Expired coupon increases order total on build 82.” Preconditions: basket total 40 and coupon expired yesterday. Steps: open checkout, enter coupon, apply. Expected: coupon rejected and total remains 40. Actual: total becomes 45. Attach the request ID and screenshot; record browser and build. This gives an investigator an actionable starting point.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A dramatic title or guessed implementation fix does not replace reproduction steps. Severity and priority may differ; a small visible issue can be urgent for a launch.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A report says “Login is bad” and includes no account state. Improve it by naming the build, account conditions, exact actions, observed message and expected result. Describe what happened before asserting a root cause.

blocks.title: Separate observations from diagnosis
blocks.text: Defect management records anomalies, analyzes and classifies them, decides actions and follows resolution status. A report may ultimately describe a product defect, test-data issue or misunderstanding. Include the object and environment, preconditions, steps, expected and actual outcomes, evidence, impact and urgency. Severity concerns consequences; priority concerns remediation timing. They can differ when a serious issue has a workaround or a small issue blocks an imminent business event. Mark suspected causes as hypotheses until supported.

blocks.title: Worked case: an actionable report
blocks.text:
Title: Refund removes the full account balance.
Build/environment: B61, staging, fixture D12, account C29.
Preconditions: payments of 40 and 70 units; balance 110.
Steps: open the 40-unit payment, choose Refund, confirm once.
Expected: refund 40, remaining balance 70.
Actual: refunded 110, remaining balance 0.
Evidence: request R88, response log, before/after screenshots.
Impact: incorrect financial amount; high severity. Priority: assessed with release owner. Status: new, awaiting triage.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Improve “Refund API is broken because the developer reused the wrong variable.” The observed refund is 300 instead of 30 on B72. How should the claimed cause be handled?

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Record payment/account state, build/environment, exact request steps, expected 30, actual 300, logs, identifiers and timestamps. Explain impact and let triage assess urgency. Treat the variable claim as a hypothesis unless investigation supports it. Reproduction and decisions should not depend on an unverified implementation diagnosis.

blocks.title: Syllabus references
blocks.text: CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, section 5.5 (starts on p. 56). Learning objectives: FL-5.5.1 (K3). Read the full section and the chapter keyword list alongside this lesson.

lessons.title: 6.1 · Tool support
lessons.summary: Match tools to activities and understand the evidence and limitations of each category.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Tools can support management, static analysis, design and implementation, execution, comparison of results, performance measurement, coverage, collaboration and delivery pipelines. Select tools for the activity and the information needed. Test-management tools organize cases, execution and reporting. Static analysis examines work products without running the software. Execution tools run checks and compare observations with expectations. Performance tools generate load and gather timing and resource evidence. Tools improve efficiency only when processes, skills and integration support their use.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: An execution harness runs service checks; a coverage tool reports unvisited branches; a performance tool creates concurrent traffic; a management tool connects cases and results to requirements. These tools answer different questions and can exchange data.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A tool does not remove the need to choose useful tests or interpret results. Recording a workflow alone does not produce a robust oracle.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which tool fits identifying unreachable code before execution? Static analysis. Which fits organizing release coverage and linking failures to cases? Test management.

blocks.title: Select support for the activity and evidence
blocks.text: Management tools organize basis, cases, execution and defects. Static tools inspect work products; design and implementation tools assist derivation and data generation. Execution tools run checks and compare outcomes; coverage tools measure reached implementation. Non-functional tools generate load or collect runtime measurements. DevOps tools support build/delivery workflows; collaboration tools share findings. Virtual machines and containers support repeatable environments. A spreadsheet can be a test tool when used for cases or expected-result calculations. Purpose determines the useful category.

blocks.title: Worked case: message processing
blocks.text: Use tracking tools for requirement/result links, static analysis for code rules, data generation for varied messages, an execution harness for comparisons, load tools for throughput and coverage tools for reached code. A controlled substitute gives repeatable dependency behavior but does not establish correctness of the real partner interface. Record tool configuration when it affects outcomes.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Choose tool categories for unreachable code, many valid customer records, concurrent response-time measurements and linked defect status.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Static analysis supports unreachable-code investigation. Data-generation/design/implementation support supplies records. Non-functional tools support load and timings. Management or defect tracking maintains status and links. Assess fit, integration and data suitability; a tool name alone does not establish quality or adequate coverage.

blocks.title: Syllabus references
blocks.text: CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, section 6.1 (starts on p. 59). Learning objectives: FL-6.1.1 (K2). Read the full section and the chapter keyword list alongside this lesson.

lessons.title: 6.2 · Automation benefits and risks
lessons.summary: Evaluate automation benefits, maintenance costs, pilot effort and unreliable signals.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Automation can make repeated checks faster and more consistent, reduce manual repetition, enable unattended execution and provide rapid feedback. Costs include implementation, maintenance, training and infrastructure. Risks include unrealistic expectations, poorly chosen checks, fragile dependencies, incorrect oracles, flaky results and overreliance on tool output. Use a pilot to learn integration costs and evaluate value. Preserve human investigation, exploratory work and judgment where they add evidence. Automated passing checks mean that the implemented checks passed under their conditions.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A stable API regression suite gives feedback on each commit. A recorded interface script fails after harmless layout changes and takes hours to maintain. The team moves checks to an appropriate layer and retains a smaller set of user workflow checks.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: More automated tests does not automatically mean better coverage. Maintenance effort and signal reliability belong in the business case.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A tool produces many false alarms. Is faster execution enough to justify it? No: consider investigation and maintenance costs. A useful pilot measures reliable feedback and value, not just the number of scripts generated.

blocks.title: Assess benefits and costs throughout adoption
blocks.text: Automation can reduce repetition, improve consistency, speed feedback and support difficult measurements. Initial costs include training, integration, scripts, environment and data. Continuing costs include maintenance and investigating unreliable results. Risks include unsuitable scope, fragile dependencies, flawed oracles and overconfidence in passing output. A representative pilot reveals practical benefits and costs. Investigate flaky outcomes: unreliable signals weaken release decisions even when retries become green. Human exploration and interpretation remain useful.

blocks.title: Worked case: a pilot effort estimate
blocks.text: Manual effort is two hours per run. Automation costs 20 hours initially and 0.5 hour upkeep per run; execution effort is negligible for this estimate. Manual effort after n runs is 2n; automated effort is 20+0.5n. Equality occurs at n=20/1.5, about 13.3; effort savings begin with the 14th run under these assumptions. Include infrastructure, changes and investigation when evaluating a real pilot, along with signal quality and scope.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A pipeline check passes on retry with no code change. The team proposes retrying until green. Name causes to investigate and explain why the rerun is insufficient evidence.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Investigate timing races, shared or unstable data, environment dependence and external-service behavior. Preserve the failure and rerun conditions. A green retry can hide an intermittent product defect or unreliable check; it does not explain the original observation. Improve isolation and diagnosis, and communicate uncertainty until resolved.

blocks.title: Syllabus references
blocks.text: CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, section 6.2 (starts on p. 59). Learning objectives: FL-6.2.1 (K1). Read the full section and the chapter keyword list alongside this lesson.

lessons.title: Final revision · Turn evidence into a study decision
lessons.summary: Review distinctions, calculations and timed-exam strategy.

blocks.title: Recall and distinguish
blocks.text: Explain testing versus debugging; error versus defect versus failure; analysis versus design versus implementation; test level versus test type; confirmation versus regression; static versus dynamic; statement versus branch coverage; entry versus exit criteria; severity versus priority; project versus product risk. Give a concrete example for each distinction rather than memorizing a label.

blocks.title: Technique checklist
blocks.text: For EP, list valid and invalid partitions before choosing representatives. For BVA, state whether two or three values are required and the input resolution. For decision tables, enumerate feasible rules before merging. For state models, count states and transitions separately. For estimation, show the formula and units. For prioritization, check dependencies and additional coverage. For defect reports, specify reproducible actions and observable expected results.

blocks.title: Timed strategy
blocks.text: Read selection counts carefully. Make one pass through straightforward items and leave time for longer application questions. Use the exact information and technique named in the question. Unanswered items score zero. Answers and explanations become available after submitting the mock or when its timer expires.

blocks.title: Review after a paper
blocks.text: For each mistake, identify the objective, explain why the chosen option failed, solve the relevant lesson example again and write a new example. Treat guesses as review targets even when correct. Use objective practice for weak areas. A repeated paper is useful revision but cannot supply fresh readiness evidence. Confirm registration and exam arrangements with your provider.

blocks.title: Explain six linked decisions
blocks.text: Choose an unfamiliar feature and explain its basis and objectives; suitable levels and types; one static evaluation; derivation and named coverage items; risk-based priority and reporting; and tool support with its limitations. Link your decisions. Duplicate-charge risk can motivate payment-rule review, retry-state checks, appropriate independence, transaction evidence and reporting of residual risk.
