Revisit objective lessons when you cannot explain a link.

blocks.title: Review calculations by their denominator
blocks.text: EP: exercised partitions / identified partitions. BVA: exercised coverage values / identified values for the stated variant. Decision tables: exercised feasible rules / feasible rules. Structural metrics: exercised statements or branches / identified statements or branches. Expected effort: (O+4M+P)/6; uncertainty estimate: (P-O)/6. State the model and units first. For prioritization, distinguish total coverage from additional coverage after previous selections.

questions.prompt: Which activity is a typical objective of testing?

options.text: Assigning development salaries
Negotiating office rental terms
Selecting the product's sales channel
Providing evidence for a release decision

questions.explanation: Testing supplies information about quality and risk for stakeholder decisions. Salaries, sales channels and rental agreements are organizational activities rather than typical test objectives. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.1 (p. 15); FL-1.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: What does the whole-team approach make a shared responsibility?

options.text: Formal inspection moderation
Product quality
Signing supplier contracts
Performance-tool administration

questions.explanation: The team shares responsibility for quality and brings complementary skills. Specific specialist duties and commercial sign-off do not become collective obligations merely because the team uses this approach. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.2 (p. 22); FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A developer investigates a failing calculation, identifies a wrong operator and repairs it. Which activity is being described?

options.text: Test monitoring
Debugging
Acceptance testing
Test analysis

questions.explanation: Debugging locates and removes a failure's cause. Analysis identifies conditions to test, monitoring compares progress with plans, and acceptance testing evaluates readiness for stakeholder use. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.2 (p. 16); FL-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A reporting product passes every written requirement but users cannot produce the report needed for their daily work. Which principle best explains the problem?

options.text: Tests wear out
Absence-of-defects fallacy
Defect clustering
Early testing saves resources

questions.explanation: Meeting specified requirements does not ensure that a product meets user needs. The stem concerns usefulness, rather than clustered defects, repeated tests or when testing begins. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.3 (p. 17); FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester studies a billing specification and identifies conditions that need checking. Which activity is the main focus?

options.text: Test implementation
Test completion
Test execution
Test analysis

questions.explanation: Analysis determines what to test from the basis. Implementation prepares procedures and environments, execution runs checks, and completion consolidates and archives outcomes. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.1 (p. 18); FL-1.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A safety-critical device and a disposable game prototype use different test approaches. What best explains this choice?

options.text: Risk, regulation and constraints shape the method
Their teams must use identical exit criteria
Their source-code languages define all testing needs
Their release dates determine the correctness of results

questions.explanation: Testing depends on context, including risk, regulation, stakeholders and resources. A language or date alone cannot determine the entire approach, and identical criteria need not suit both products. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.2 (p. 19); FL-1.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which testware is most directly created when preparing an ordered procedure for running several test cases?

options.text: A defect status summary
A test completion report
A product risk register
A test script

questions.explanation: An execution procedure or script is implementation testware. Risks support planning; completion reports summarize finished work; defect status summaries concern findings rather than executable steps. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.3 (p. 20); FL-1.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester needs to discuss a reproducible failure with its author. Which response best demonstrates constructive communication?

options.text: Delay the report until a different tester can present it
Rank the author's competence in the defect title
State a root cause before investigating the failure
Give observable outcomes and concrete steps to repeat the issue

questions.explanation: Specific observations and reproduction steps support investigation without blame. Personal criticism, unsupported diagnosis and unnecessary delay undermine useful communication. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.1 (p. 21); FL-1.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which testing practice is useful across development lifecycles?

options.text: Replace component checks with stakeholder acceptance
Wait for implementation to end before designing checks
Give component and system testing identical objectives
Review suitable draft requirements and designs early

questions.explanation: Early review can prevent downstream defects across lifecycles. Delaying all testing, replacing lower-level checks or using identical objectives at every level removes useful evidence. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 25); FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which approach begins with component tests before writing the corresponding implementation?

options.text: Test-driven development
Risk-based testing
Checklist-based testing
Exploratory testing

questions.explanation: TDD uses a failing component test to guide implementation and refactoring. Exploratory testing integrates learning and execution; risk-based testing prioritizes by risk; checklists guide conditions to inspect. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 26); FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: A team checks interactions between a tax-calculation component and a pricing component within one application. Which level is the primary focus?

options.text: System integration testing
Acceptance testing
Component integration testing
Component testing

questions.explanation: Component integration targets interactions among components. Component testing isolates a component; system integration concerns interactions among systems; acceptance assesses stakeholder readiness. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.1 (p. 28); FL-2.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A fix corrects the original tax-rounding failure. Why also run previously passing discount tests?

options.text: To diagnose the operator that caused the original defect
To detect unintended effects of the change
To replace confirmation testing of the repaired behavior
To establish that no defects remain in the application

questions.explanation: Regression testing checks for adverse effects on existing behavior. Diagnosis belongs to debugging; a passing suite cannot prove absence of defects, and confirmation of the fix remains useful. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.3 (p. 30); FL-2.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: An application is delivered in small increments. Which test planning response is appropriate?

options.text: Reuse the first increment's cases without reviewing changes
Limit every iteration to acceptance testing of new features
Postpone design of test cases until the final increment
Test each increment and consider regression of existing behavior

questions.explanation: Incremental development needs checks of new behavior and potentially affected existing behavior. Waiting until the end or ignoring changes loses timely feedback; one level cannot address every risk. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 25); FL-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A DevOps pipeline gives rapid automated feedback, but intermittently reports failures caused by unstable test data. What should the team address?

options.text: The removal of all manual investigation
The use of slower deployments as the sole quality measure
Stabilize the data and improve signal reliability
The replacement of every review with pipeline execution

questions.explanation: Unreliable feedback consumes investigation effort and reduces trust. DevOps still needs human judgment and reviews; deployment speed alone does not establish quality. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.4 (p. 26); FL-2.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which work product can be assessed through static testing before any executable application exists?

options.text: An execution of the application's binary
A live session exercising implemented checkout behavior
A draft user story
A measured production response-time trace generated by the new application

questions.explanation: A user story can be reviewed without executing the software. The other choices depend on execution or implemented behavior and describe runtime evidence or activity. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.1 (p. 33); FL-3.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: What is a benefit of early stakeholder feedback on a draft workflow?

options.text: Discovering mismatched expectations before implementation
Replacing the need for an agreed test basis
Eliminating the need to assess implemented behavior
Guaranteeing that stakeholders will never change priorities

questions.explanation: Feedback can expose misunderstanding while changes are cheaper. It neither prevents future changes nor removes dynamic testing or the need for shared expectations. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.1 (p. 35); FL-3.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A review finds contradictory fee rules before coding starts. Why does this add value?

options.text: It can prevent implementing inconsistent behavior
It proves that the future implementation has no defects
It demonstrates runtime performance under peak load
It replaces the need to test fee calculations after coding

questions.explanation: Early defect detection can avoid rework and failures downstream. A requirements review does not measure runtime performance, certify future code or replace complementary dynamic checks. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.2 (p. 33); FL-3.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Reviewers have individually recorded anomalies in a design. What is the next main review activity?

options.text: Communicate and analyze the findings
Archive the final test execution logs
Skip to closure without evaluating anomalies
Deploy the implementation to production

questions.explanation: After individual review, participants discuss and analyze anomalies before fixing and reporting. Deployment and execution logs are unrelated steps; unresolved findings should not simply be ignored. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.2 (p. 35); FL-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO examples of black-box test derivation.

options.text: Choose a case because a similar product once failed there
Choose cases from combinations of business-rule conditions
Choose a case to execute an unvisited source-code branch
Choose inputs from specified valid and invalid age ranges

questions.explanation: Partitions and decision tables derive from specified behavior. An unvisited branch uses internal structure, while prior failure experience motivates error guessing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.1 (p. 39); FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: An input executes all executable statements in a function. What follows about statement coverage?

options.text: Requirements-based acceptance coverage is complete
It is 100% for that function
The business specification contains no ambiguity
That function’s false decision outcome has also run

questions.explanation: Executing all statements establishes full statement coverage. It says nothing conclusive about branch outcomes, missing requirements or correctness, so those stronger claims are unsupported. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 (p. 42); FL-4.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A decision has true and false outcomes. Existing tests exercise only the true outcome. What improves its branch coverage?

options.text: Repeat the true-outcome test with a new test name
Increase the number of assertions on the true path
Inspect the same execution log a second time
Add an input that takes the unvisited path

questions.explanation: The missing branch is the false outcome; executing it improves coverage. Renaming, rereading or adding assertions on an already exercised path does not execute a new branch. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 (p. 43); FL-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester adds cases for empty input after recalling earlier validation defects. Which technique is being used?

options.text: State transition testing
Statement testing
Error guessing
Decision table testing

questions.explanation: The choice is driven by experience with likely errors. No structural coverage, condition table or state model is used to derive the case in this scenario. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 (p. 43); FL-4.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: During a chartered session, each observation guides the tester's next experiment. Which technique best fits?

options.text: A formal inspection meeting
Exploratory testing
Three-point estimation
A fixed scripted regression run

questions.explanation: Exploratory testing combines learning, design and execution adaptively. Fixed scripts predefine the sequence; inspections review work products; estimation predicts effort rather than explores behavior. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 (p. 44); FL-4.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Business, development and testing discuss concrete examples for a user story. What is the main benefit?

options.text: A replacement for evaluation of completed functionality
A prescribed internal implementation for the agreed examples
A shared understanding of desired behavior
An implementation design sufficient to bypass reviews

questions.explanation: Collaboration clarifies needs and exposes differing assumptions. It need not dictate implementation and cannot guarantee defect-free requirements or remove later evaluation. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 (p. 45); FL-4.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A field accepts integer ages 18–65 inclusive. Values below 18 and above 65 are rejected for different reasons. Which set covers every stated equivalence partition?
questions.explanation: The three partitions are below 18, valid 18–65 and above 65. The correct set represents each. The other sets omit one or both invalid partitions; boundary coverage is not the requested measure. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: An integer quantity is accepted from 3 through 7. Which set supplies two-value boundary analysis for both edges?
questions.explanation: Two-value BVA checks each boundary and its immediate adjacent-partition neighbor: 2/3 and 7/8. Interior neighbors belong to three-value coverage; distant values skip the nearest neighbors. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A discount is granted when an account is active AND a coupon is valid. Both conditions can independently be true or false. How many feasible rules are needed in the full, unminimized decision table?
questions.explanation: Two independent Boolean conditions give 2 × 2 = 4 combinations. One permits a discount and three deny it. Counting actions alone gives two, while eight would require a third independent Boolean condition. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 (p. 41); FL-4.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Model: Locked --coin→ Unlocked; Unlocked --push→ Locked; Locked --push→ Locked; Unlocked --coin→ Unlocked. Starting Locked, events coin,push have run. What is valid-transition coverage?
questions.explanation: Two of the four specified valid transitions ran: Locked→Unlocked on coin and Unlocked→Locked on push. Both states were visited, but the two self-transitions were not, so state coverage must not be substituted. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 (p. 41); FL-4.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Criterion: orders totaling at least 50 receive free delivery; lower totals cost 5. Which TWO acceptance examples test the threshold correctly?

options.text: Total 50 expects delivery charge 0
Total 49.99 expects delivery charge 0
Total 50 expects delivery charge 5
Total 49.99 expects delivery charge 5

questions.explanation: The rule includes 50 in the free-delivery class. The neighboring lower total stays in the paid class. The distractors reverse the expected results and would encode the wrong business rule. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: How can a tester contribute during iteration planning?

options.text: Replace the product owner in ranking business value
Identify testability concerns and testing effort
Approve supplier invoices for the release
Set the organization's annual salary bands

questions.explanation: Testers contribute testing expertise, feasibility and effort information to planning. Commercial administration and business prioritization ownership are different responsibilities. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.2 (p. 48); FL-5.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A team needs a document defining test scope, approach, resources and completion criteria. Which testware serves that purpose?

options.text: A test execution log
An automated test result
An individual defect report
A test plan

questions.explanation: A plan describes intended testing and its organization. Logs and results capture executed work; defect reports describe anomalies rather than the overall approach and resource commitments. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.1 (p. 48); FL-5.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which activity best fits the business-facing quadrant that critiques the product (Q3)?

options.text: Load testing of service throughput
Acceptance examples guiding implementation
Exploratory usability evaluation with users
Automated component checks of an internal function

questions.explanation: Q3 evaluates the product from a business or user perspective. Component checks fit Q1, technical performance evaluation fits Q4, and implementation-guiding acceptance examples fit Q2. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which is a product risk rather than a project risk?

options.text: The released application calculates interest incorrectly
The test environment arrives two weeks late
A key tester becomes unavailable during the schedule
The supplier misses a planned handover date

questions.explanation: Incorrect interest is a potential product-quality problem. Staffing, environment delivery and supplier delays threaten execution of the project and its schedule. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.2 (p. 52); FL-5.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A release manager needs to decide whether to ship. Which report content is most useful?

options.text: The number of team meetings without testing outcomes
Achieved coverage, unresolved defects and residual risks
The names of test tools without their results
Every raw request log without an interpretation

questions.explanation: Decision-makers need evidence and its implications, including gaps and risk. Raw logs, meeting counts and tool names alone do not communicate readiness to release. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.2 (p. 54); FL-5.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why link an execution result to build, test-suite and data-set versions?

options.text: To avoid recording actual and expected results
To remove the need for impact analysis on changes
To make the evidence reproducible and attributable
To establish that later builds have identical behavior

questions.explanation: Configuration references identify what was tested and help reproduce findings. They do not replace result details, imply unchanged later builds or remove analysis of changes. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Use E=(O+4M+P)/6. An effort estimate has O=4, M=7 and P=16 hours. What is E?

options.text: 7 hours
8 hours
9 hours
12 hours

questions.explanation: Substitution gives (4+28+16)/6=48/6=8 hours. Seven uses only the most-likely value; nine is the unweighted mean; twelve does not follow the specified formula. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: For additional-coverage prioritization, T1 covers A,B,C; T2 covers B,C; T3 covers D,E. No dependencies apply. Which order is correct?
questions.explanation: T1 first adds three items. T3 next adds two still-uncovered items, while T2 adds none. Static total-coverage ordering would incorrectly place T2 second for the requested additional-coverage technique. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: A report for a checkout failure already includes build, browser, account state and steps. Which addition most directly makes the anomaly evaluable?

options.text: Actual and expected totals linked to the pricing rule
A proposed database rewrite without observed outcomes
A list of unrelated defects from another product
A personal assessment of the developer's skill

questions.explanation: Specific actual and expected results tied to the basis let an investigator evaluate the anomaly. Proposed fixes, personal criticism and unrelated findings do not establish what failed. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team needs to simulate concurrent users and measure response time. Which tool category is appropriate?

options.text: Performance testing tools
Configuration management tools
Test data cataloging tools
Static analysis tools

questions.explanation: Performance tools generate load and collect timing or resource evidence. Configuration tools version items, static analysis inspects work products, and catalogs organize data rather than measure behavior under load. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO potential benefits of suitable test automation.

options.text: Proof that no defects remain
Rapid feedback after code changes
Elimination of test maintenance
Repeatable execution of routine checks

questions.explanation: Automation can execute repeatable checks and provide quick feedback. Scripts and infrastructure still need maintenance, and their passing results do not prove absence of defects. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: How is testing commonly classified in relation to quality management?

options.text: A process-oriented quality-assurance audit
A product-oriented quality-control activity
A commercial product-positioning activity
A personnel performance-appraisal activity

questions.explanation: Testing evaluates work products and their quality, making it quality control. QA focuses on processes; commercial positioning and employee appraisal are not its classification. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.2 (p. 17); FL-1.2.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: What is an advantage of testers, developers and business representatives working as one team?

options.text: Assigning quality ownership exclusively to the testers
Combining complementary skills to solve quality problems
Making each person equally proficient in every tool
Removing the need for any specialized test knowledge

questions.explanation: Complementary skills improve problem solving and shared understanding. Whole-team working neither gives everyone identical expertise nor removes specialization; quality remains shared. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.2 (p. 22); FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A hospital system is tested before a medication workflow is released. Which reason most directly justifies the effort?

options.text: Replace the need for review of medication requirements
Transfer responsibility for medical decisions to testers
Establish that every possible input has been exercised
Reduce the chance of harmful failures reaching users

questions.explanation: Testing provides evidence and reduces delivery risk, which matters where failures may harm users. Exhaustive testing is generally infeasible, and testing does not assume clinical responsibility or replace reviews. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.1 (p. 16); FL-1.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team reviews draft requirements before coding and resolves unclear rules. Which principle does this illustrate?

options.text: Tests wear out
Defects cluster together
Early testing saves time and money
Testing shows the absence of defects

questions.explanation: Resolving problems early avoids downstream implementation and rework. The situation does not involve repeated tests or clustering, and testing cannot establish absence of defects. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.3 (p. 17); FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly links an activity to its typical testware?

options.text: Completion — new input partitions as its main output
Analysis — production deployment binaries
Planning — measured results from tests not yet executed
Execution — logs of observed outcomes

questions.explanation: Execution creates records of observations. Conditions and partitions concern analysis/design; binaries are implementation products of development; planning cannot record outcomes of future execution. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.3 (p. 20); FL-1.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A requirement changes, and links from it to cases identify which checks need revision. What benefit is being used?

options.text: Proof that all unlinked requirements are covered
Removal of the need to review the revised requirement
Impact assessment through traceability
Automatic repair of defects in the implementation

questions.explanation: Traceability enables impact analysis by relating basis and testware. Links do not perform reviews or code repairs, and absent links cannot prove coverage. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.4 (p. 20); FL-1.4.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: A small team member schedules testing and also derives cases. How should the roles be understood?

options.text: An individual can carry both responsibilities
Case derivation makes all scheduling a development role
The person must choose one role and abandon the other
Roles require different people even in a small team

questions.explanation: Roles describe responsibilities and can be combined. Scheduling is test management and derivation is technical testing; neither changes category because the same person performs it. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.5 (p. 21); FL-1.4.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: An independent tester challenges assumptions shared by the authors. What benefit does this illustrate?

options.text: Independent testers own all product quality
Independent testing makes communication unnecessary
A different perspective can reveal overlooked problems
Author-created checks lose all value once independence is added

questions.explanation: Independence can expose shared assumptions. Collaboration and shared quality responsibility still matter, and developer checks continue to provide useful evidence. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.3 (p. 22); FL-1.5.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement describes good coordination of development and testing?

options.text: Every development activity requires only production monitoring
Testers should avoid draft work products until sign-off
Testing activities should share one identical objective
Each test level has objectives suited to that level

questions.explanation: Different levels address different objects and goals. One objective for all levels loses their distinctions; production monitoring alone omits earlier evidence, and suitable drafts can be reviewed. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 25); FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which approach expresses expected behavior as business-readable scenarios before implementing it?

options.text: Behavior-driven development
Defect density analysis
Configuration baselining
Behavior-based coverage measurement

questions.explanation: BDD uses behavior-focused examples, often in Given/When/Then form, to guide shared understanding and development. Coverage, defect metrics and baselines serve different purposes. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 26); FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: A service is checked for response time and resource usage under peak traffic. Which type of testing is the main focus?

options.text: Non-functional testing
Confirmation testing
Functional rule testing
Static requirements review

questions.explanation: Timing and resource characteristics are non-functional qualities. Confirmation concerns a specific fix; functional testing checks what the system does; static review cannot measure live load behavior. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.2 (p. 29); FL-2.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: The application code is unchanged, but its database platform is upgraded. What testing response is appropriate?

options.text: Treat the upgrade as outside all testing responsibilities
Assume a previously passing result applies to the new platform
Run only the first component test ever written
Assess affected behavior and perform maintenance testing

questions.explanation: Platform changes can affect queries, data and integrations even without source changes. Impact analysis guides maintenance scope; arbitrary tests or old evidence do not establish compatibility. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.3 (p. 31); FL-2.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A retrospective agrees an improvement but assigns no owner or follow-up. What should be added?

options.text: An actionable experiment with ownership and outcome review
A guarantee that the same issue cannot recur
A restriction to measuring individual performance
A replacement of all technical discussion with voting

questions.explanation: Retrospectives should produce useful improvements and assess their effects. Guarantees, eliminating discussion or blaming individuals do not make actions effective. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.6 (p. 28); FL-2.1.6 (K2).

questions.prompt: Reviewing acceptance examples during refinement instead of waiting for completed code is an example of what?

options.text: Delaying feedback until the release decision
Moving suitable testing earlier
Replacing system testing with code review
Moving all checks into production

questions.explanation: Shift left moves suitable activities earlier, including review of examples. It complements rather than replaces later testing and does not mean shifting work into production or postponing feedback. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.5 (p. 27); FL-2.1.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which review role primarily facilitates an effective review meeting?

options.text: Manager
Scribe
Author
Moderator

questions.explanation: The moderator facilitates communication and keeps the meeting useful. The author creates the artifact, the scribe records findings and management provides resources and support. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.3 (p. 36); FL-3.2.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which factor contributes to a successful review?

options.text: The artifact is as large as possible for every session
Findings are discouraged to protect the schedule
Participants prepare against clear objectives
The meeting evaluates the author's personal worth

questions.explanation: Preparation and clear aims support meaningful evaluation. Personal appraisal, oversized artifacts and suppressing findings undermine effectiveness and constructive feedback. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.5 (p. 37); FL-3.2.5 (K1).

questions.prompt: Select TWO accurate distinctions between static and dynamic testing.

options.text: Static review can find ambiguity in an unimplemented requirement
Dynamic testing identifies defects directly without observing execution
Dynamic testing executes software to observe behavior
Static testing measures live throughput by running the application

questions.explanation: Static testing examines artifacts without execution and can reveal ambiguity. Dynamic testing observes behavior through execution; live throughput is dynamic and failure observations may need further diagnosis. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.3 (p. 34); FL-3.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A review is author-led and takes participants through a work product to build understanding and gather findings. Which review type best fits?

options.text: Walkthrough
Inspection
Performance benchmark
Static analysis scan

questions.explanation: Walkthroughs are typically led by the author and can educate participants or find anomalies. Inspections are more formally organized; scans and benchmarks are tool or execution activities rather than this review type. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.4 (p. 36); FL-3.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester derives cases from source-code control flow. What makes these white-box cases?

options.text: They are written by the original developer
They are necessarily automated
Their coverage items come from internal structure
They require a user representative to choose inputs

questions.explanation: The basis for derivation defines the technique family. Automation, author identity and stakeholder participation do not by themselves make a case white-box. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.1 (p. 39); FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A function runs both outcomes of each modeled conditional decision. What evidence is established?

options.text: Consistent behavior in future configurations
Full branch coverage
Completion of requirements-based acceptance
Execution of each input-data combination

questions.explanation: Executing both outcomes covers the corresponding branches. It does not exhaust input combinations, detect omitted functionality or guarantee behavior in other environments. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 (p. 43); FL-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: An implementation omits a required surcharge rule entirely, yet its existing code reaches 100% branch coverage. What is the limitation?

options.text: Reachable code can still omit required business rules
Full branch coverage includes absent requirements
The omission makes coverage calculations undefined
Branch coverage measures stakeholder satisfaction

questions.explanation: Coverage measures the structure that exists. A missing business rule needs requirements-based evidence; neither coverage alone nor stakeholder satisfaction can be inferred from code reachability. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 (p. 43); FL-4.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team organizes exploratory testing around 60-minute charters. What should it retain for useful accountability?

options.text: A claim of complete requirements coverage
Observations, tested areas and a session debrief
A fixed sequence that forbids adapting to discoveries
The count of mouse clicks made

questions.explanation: Charters and recorded observations make exploration communicable. Click counts do not describe coverage, universal coverage claims are unsupported, and adapting to findings is central to exploration. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 (p. 44); FL-4.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester uses a list of common accessibility and validation conditions, choosing detailed inputs during execution. Which technique fits?

options.text: A formal decision table
Checklist-based testing
A fully specified execution script
Branch coverage analysis

questions.explanation: The list guides what to check while leaving detailed cases to judgment. A script prescribes steps more tightly; branches and decision tables derive from different coverage models. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 (p. 44); FL-4.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO valid styles for documenting acceptance criteria.

options.text: Private implementation guesses unrelated to needs
Scenario-oriented examples
Rule-oriented constraints
Unverifiable statements of enthusiasm

questions.explanation: Scenarios and rules can express evaluable behavior. Enthusiasm without observable conditions and irrelevant implementation guesses do not give dependable acceptance criteria. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 (p. 45); FL-4.5.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: An input has four specified equivalence partitions. A suite exercises representatives of three different partitions. What is its equivalence-partition coverage?
questions.explanation: Coverage is exercised partitions divided by total partitions: 3/4 × 100 = 75%. The number of values within each exercised partition does not alter this measure; the fourth partition remains uncovered. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A temperature accepts integers 10–20 inclusive. Considering the valid partition boundary values 10 and 20, which set exercises each of these values and both of its immediate neighbors?
questions.explanation: For the specified valid-partition boundaries, exercise 9/10/11 and 19/20/21. Four points omit their inside neighbors; distant or exclusively valid points miss stated coverage items. This question targets boundary values 10 and 20; full three-value coverage across all partition boundaries would also include 8 and 22. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: Rule: a member receives a discount regardless of coupon; a non-member receives it only with a valid coupon. Which TWO combinations receive a discount?

options.text: Non-member with no valid coupon
Member with no coupon
Non-member with a valid coupon
Non-member with an invalid coupon

questions.explanation: Membership alone grants the discount; a valid coupon grants it to a non-member. Both non-member distractors lack a valid coupon, so the specified rule denies the discount. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 (p. 41); FL-4.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: States are Draft, Submitted and Approved. Valid transitions are Draft→Submitted, Submitted→Draft and Submitted→Approved. Starting Draft, a test submits then approves. Which uncovered transition must another test exercise for full valid-transition coverage?

options.text: Return from Approved to Draft
Move from Draft directly to Approved
Move from Approved to Submitted
Return from Submitted to Draft

questions.explanation: Submit then approve covers two of the three listed transitions. The remaining valid transition is Submitted→Draft. The other transitions are not defined as valid in this model. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 (p. 41); FL-4.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Criterion: after three consecutive failed logins, an account locks; a successful login before lock resets the count. Which sequence tests the reset behavior?

options.text: Fail, succeed, fail; account becomes locked
Fail, fail, succeed, fail; account remains unlocked
Succeed, fail, fail; account becomes locked
Fail, fail, fail; account remains unlocked

questions.explanation: The successful third attempt resets the count, so the final failure is the first of a new sequence. Three consecutive failures should lock; one or two failures after reset should not. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Which distribution best reflects the test pyramid?

options.text: A ban on testing user workflows
Many small checks and fewer broad end-to-end checks
The same number of checks at every scope
Few component checks and many broad end-to-end checks

questions.explanation: The pyramid encourages a broad base of small, fast checks and a smaller set of broad checks. It does not demand identical counts or eliminate end-to-end evidence. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.6 (p. 50); FL-5.1.6 (K1).

questions.prompt: An environment must be ready before system execution begins; an agreed defect threshold must be met before it finishes. How are these criteria classified?

options.text: Both are exit because they refer to quality
Environment readiness is entry; defect threshold is exit
Environment readiness is exit; defect threshold is entry
Both are entry because they refer to testing

questions.explanation: Entry conditions enable starting an activity; exit conditions enable completion. Their function, rather than the words “environment” or “defect,” determines the classification. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.3 (p. 49); FL-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A load test critiques throughput using technical measures. Which testing quadrant best fits?

options.text: Q1: technology-facing support for development
Q4: technology-facing product evaluation
Q2: business-facing support for development
Q3: business-facing product evaluation

questions.explanation: Load and technical performance evaluation belong in Q4. Q1 concerns development-supporting technical checks; Q2 acceptance examples support work; Q3 assesses business-facing product use. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: A payment failure has greater assessed product risk than a cosmetic issue. How should that influence testing?

options.text: Treat the risk ranking as proof of a future failure
Delete every test outside the payment area
Use the same effort regardless of risk differences
Investigate payment behavior more thoroughly

questions.explanation: Risk analysis guides effort, techniques and scope. It need not eliminate all lower-risk checks, ignore differences or predict with certainty that a failure will occur. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.3 (p. 52); FL-5.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A remote release team includes engineers and business managers. How should test status be communicated?

options.text: Use a private conversation instead of an accessible record
Send unexplained logs and expect similar interpretation
Summarize implications and link technical detail
Omit blocked cases until test execution has finished

questions.explanation: Different audiences need different detail; shared summaries and linked evidence support understanding. Unexplained logs, private-only discussion and hidden blockers undermine informed decisions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.3 (p. 55); FL-5.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A rerun uses updated data with the same build and test procedure and now passes. What configuration information is essential to interpret the change?

options.text: The number of unused accounts in a different release
The office location where the first report was written
The alphabetical ordering of tester names
The versions of both data sets

questions.explanation: Data changes can affect reproducibility and conclusions. Recording versions lets investigators compare conditions; irrelevant administrative or unrelated counts do not explain the changed outcome. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Historical testing effort is 25% of development effort for comparable work. Development is estimated at 160 hours. Using that ratio, what is the testing estimate?

options.text: 120 hours
64 hours
40 hours
25 hours

questions.explanation: The ratio gives 0.25 × 160 = 40 hours. Twenty-five treats a percentage as hours; sixty-four uses the wrong ratio; 120 is the remaining share rather than testing effort. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Risk priorities are Payment highest, Search medium, Profile lowest. Payment requires Account Setup first. No other dependencies apply. Which ordering honors risk and dependencies?

options.text: Payment, Account Setup, Search, Profile
Account Setup, Payment, Search, Profile
Profile, Search, Account Setup, Payment
Search, Profile, Payment, Account Setup

questions.explanation: Setup must precede Payment even though Payment has the highest risk. Once the prerequisite is met, Payment comes before medium and low risk. The other orders violate dependency or unnecessarily defer the highest risk. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: A mobile crash occurs only for an offline session with a cached cart. Which defect-report precondition is most useful?

options.text: The reporter likes the application interface
The developer should rewrite the cache immediately
The team has tested another device in an unrelated release
Identify build, device, network mode and stored cart data

questions.explanation: These conditions help reproduce the particular crash. Opinion, a proposed fix and unrelated evidence do not establish the setup that triggers the observed failure. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tool flags unreachable code and coding-rule violations without executing the application. Which category fits?

options.text: Performance testing
Test execution
Service virtualization
Static analysis

questions.explanation: Static analysis inspects structured work products without running them. Performance and execution tools observe runtime behavior; virtualization supplies substitutes for dependencies rather than performs this analysis. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which risk should be considered when adopting a record-and-playback interface tool?

options.text: The certainty that every recorded action detects a defect
The inability to automate any repeatable checks
The disappearance of all execution-time savings
Maintenance costs when screen layout and controls change

questions.explanation: Interface scripts can be fragile and require maintenance after changes. This is a risk to evaluate, not a claim that automation never saves time or that every action detects a defect. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Select TWO typical test objectives.

options.text: Verify satisfaction of specified requirements
Validate suitability for stakeholder use
Prove that the product contains no defects
Set business profit targets for next year

questions.explanation: Verification and validation are testing objectives. Testing cannot prove absence of all defects; profit targets are business planning rather than evaluating work products. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.1 (p. 15); FL-1.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which practice fits a whole-team approach to quality?

options.text: Every team member must perform the same daily tasks
Testers help colleagues develop useful testing skills
Business representatives avoid acceptance discussions
Developers delegate all quality concerns to a separate team

questions.explanation: Sharing expertise helps the team contribute to quality. Delegating all quality, excluding business input or requiring identical duties contradicts complementary contributions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.2 (p. 22); FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A programmer misreads a rule, writes a wrong comparison, and an eligible customer is rejected. What is the observed rejection?

options.text: An error
A failure
A root cause
A defect

questions.explanation: The rejection is observed incorrect behavior, a failure. Misreading is the human error; the comparison is the defect; an underlying reason for the mistake would be a root cause. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.3 (p. 17); FL-1.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Most discovered defects are concentrated in two modules. Which testing response uses the clustering principle sensibly?

options.text: Attribute the defects to module size without investigation
Focus investigation there and assess remaining risks
Infer that the remaining modules are defect-free
Remove regression checks from the affected modules

questions.explanation: Clustering guides focused investigation but does not prove unexamined areas safe. Removing regression or reducing every cause to size is unsupported by the observation. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.3 (p. 17); FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Cases have been designed. The tester now prepares accounts, data and an execution sequence. Which activity is the main focus?

options.text: Test monitoring
Test analysis
Test implementation
Test completion

questions.explanation: Implementation prepares runnable testware and environments. Analysis identifies conditions, monitoring tracks progress, and completion consolidates finished work. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.1 (p. 18); FL-1.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Requirement-to-test links show that a high-risk requirement has no associated case. What does this expose?

options.text: A guarantee that adding one case will eliminate its risk
Missing planned coverage for that high-risk behavior
Proof that existing test results are incorrect
Proof that the implementation is defective

questions.explanation: Traceability can reveal missing planned coverage. The gap is not proof of a code defect or incorrect earlier results, and one case cannot guarantee removal of every associated risk. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.4 (p. 20); FL-1.4.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which task most directly belongs to the test-management role?

options.text: Prepare the detailed data for one test case
Derive individual boundary-value inputs
Coordinate resources and monitor test progress
Execute a specified API check

questions.explanation: Coordination and monitoring are management responsibilities. Input derivation, execution and detailed data preparation are technical testing activities, although one person can perform both roles. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.5 (p. 21); FL-1.4.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester examines an unexpected result and designs a follow-up to distinguish two possible explanations. Which skill is most directly demonstrated?

options.text: Personal blame attribution
Sales negotiation
Administrative invoice processing
Analytical thinking

questions.explanation: Designing evidence to distinguish explanations uses analytical reasoning. Commercial or administrative duties and blaming a person do not explain the investigative behavior. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.1 (p. 21); FL-1.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why establish objectives and an appropriate basis for each test level?

options.text: To ensure all levels find identical defects
To avoid reviewing development artifacts
To require all tests to run on production data
To focus evaluation on the purpose of its stage

questions.explanation: Objectives and a basis focus checks and expected results at each level. Levels need not find the same defect types, and neither reviews nor controlled test data are excluded. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 25); FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which approach collaboratively derives acceptance tests before implementing a user story?

options.text: Acceptance test-driven development
Acceptance coverage measurement
Defect trend monitoring
Exploratory session management

questions.explanation: ATDD uses agreed acceptance examples to guide implementation. Exploratory management organizes investigations; statement analysis evaluates structure; defect trends support monitoring. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 26); FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: A payroll application exchanges files with an external bank service. Tests check that interaction. Which level is the primary focus?

options.text: System integration testing
User acceptance testing
Component integration testing
Component testing

questions.explanation: Interactions between systems or external services are the focus of system integration. Lower levels target components; user acceptance checks readiness for stakeholder needs rather than this interface specifically. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.1 (p. 28); FL-2.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A repaired defect is checked with the inputs that originally triggered it. What is the primary purpose?

options.text: Confirmation that the specific failure no longer occurs
Replacement of checks for adverse effects elsewhere
Discovery of the developer's original reasoning mistake
Measurement of every branch in the system

questions.explanation: Confirmation testing evaluates the repaired behavior. Debugging investigates causes; branch measurement is structural coverage; regression remains needed for possible side effects. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.3 (p. 30); FL-2.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A retrospective compares promised improvement actions with results from the next iteration. Why is this useful?

options.text: Assess whether the change was effective
It replaces collecting test execution evidence
It certifies future iterations as defect-free
It imposes identical practices across different teams

questions.explanation: Reviewing effects supports evidence-based process improvement. It cannot certify future iterations, replace product testing or prescribe one process for all contexts. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.6 (p. 28); FL-2.1.6 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO ways DevOps can support testing.

options.text: Continuous deployment proves every requirement is correct
Pipeline tools eliminate the need for test design
Cross-functional collaboration reduces handover friction
Automated checks provide faster delivery feedback

questions.explanation: DevOps practices can speed feedback and improve collaboration. Deployment itself does not prove correctness, and useful automated checks still require thoughtful design. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.4 (p. 26); FL-2.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which item is suitable for a review-based static test?

options.text: A timing benchmark that runs the application
A proposed test case with expected results
An executed user session on a new binary
A live throughput experiment on a running service

questions.explanation: A test case can be reviewed as a work product, including its expectations. Throughput experiments, executed sessions and timing benchmarks run software and are dynamic activities. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.1 (p. 33); FL-3.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which review role records findings and agreed decisions during a meeting?

options.text: Scribe
Author
Moderator
Review manager

questions.explanation: The scribe documents findings and decisions. The moderator facilitates, the author owns the artifact, and management provides organizational support rather than this recording duty. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.3 (p. 36); FL-3.2.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: A review detects a missing rule; a runtime test reveals an incorrect output. Which distinction is accurate?

options.text: Both activities require executing the application
Static checks expose defects; dynamic checks expose failures
The missing rule can be found only through runtime coverage
The incorrect output is the human mistake itself

questions.explanation: Static review can directly reveal an omission. Dynamic execution produces an observed failure. Neither requires static review to run software, and the output is not itself a human error. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.3 (p. 34); FL-3.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: The review meeting has classified anomalies and agreed changes. Which activity closes the loop?

options.text: Replacing the artifact with execution logs
Starting a new review without tracking the changes
Fixing the work product and reporting follow-up results
Discarding findings after the meeting ends

questions.explanation: Fixing and reporting ensure findings lead to changes and tracked outcomes. Discarding or losing links prevents closure; execution logs are not a substitute for the reviewed artifact. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.2 (p. 35); FL-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester selects malformed dates because previous projects often mishandled them. Which family of techniques is the main basis?

options.text: Control-flow coverage
White-box
Experience-based
Black-box decision-table analysis

questions.explanation: The selection is driven by past defect experience, so it is experience-based error guessing. No structural model or explicitly analyzed condition table is given. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.1 (p. 39); FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A program has an if statement without an else, followed by a statement that runs for every input. Tests take only the true path. Why can statement coverage be complete while branch coverage is incomplete?

options.text: Branch coverage excludes conditional decisions
Statement coverage counts requirements rather than code
All statements can run without taking the false outcome
The false outcome adds an executable else statement by definition

questions.explanation: The true path can execute both the conditional body and following statement. The false outcome is still unexecuted even without an else body. Statement coverage concerns code, and decisions contribute branches. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 (p. 42); FL-4.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO appropriate interpretations of full structural coverage.

options.text: It establishes exhaustive coverage of input combinations
It can coexist with incorrect expected behavior
It provides evidence that modeled code items were exercised
It certifies implementation of omitted business rules

questions.explanation: Structural reachability is valuable but independent of whether results are correct. Missing rules and all combinations require evidence beyond the covered structure. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 (p. 43); FL-4.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester uses a fault checklist built from incidents: null input, duplicate submission and rounding errors. What is the main reason these cases were selected?

options.text: A complete table of all Boolean combinations
A requirement to execute every branch
A model of all states and transitions
Knowledge of plausible developer mistakes

questions.explanation: Incident-based fault ideas are error guessing. The stem does not describe branch coverage, a decision table or a state model as the derivation basis. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 (p. 43); FL-4.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why review and update a testing checklist after a new category of failures appears?

options.text: To keep its guidance relevant to current risks
To turn it into proof of exhaustive testing
To remove the need for observations during execution
To forbid testers from using judgment

questions.explanation: A checklist evolves with risks and experience. Updating it neither guarantees completeness nor removes judgment and recording of actual behavior. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 (p. 44); FL-4.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A user story states a requested feature but omits why the user needs it. What should the conversation clarify?

options.text: The exact database table names before discussing behavior
The tester's preferred automation framework
The total number of future regression scripts
The user's goal and the value of the capability

questions.explanation: Understanding user value helps judge desired behavior and examples. Implementation names, framework preferences and speculative script counts do not resolve the missing need. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 (p. 45); FL-4.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A form has three payment-method partitions and two delivery-method partitions. Every combination is feasible. What is the minimum number of cases to cover each partition of both inputs, without requiring combination coverage?
questions.explanation: Three cases can cover the three payment partitions and include both delivery partitions, for example P1/D1, P2/D2 and P3/D1. Two cannot cover three payment partitions; six covers all combinations, a stronger requirement than stated. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A balance rule accepts amounts 100.00–200.00 inclusive, with resolution 0.01. Which pair checks the lower boundary using two-value BVA?
questions.explanation: The boundary is 100.00 and the closest point across it is 99.99 at the stated resolution. Interior neighbors apply to three-value analysis; one-unit jumps are not immediate neighbors. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: Access requires authentication and either admin status or an active subscription. Which TWO cases are permitted?

options.text: Unauthenticated admin with active subscription
Authenticated non-admin without subscription
Authenticated non-admin with active subscription
Authenticated admin without subscription

questions.explanation: Authentication is mandatory. After it, either admin status or active subscription suffices. One distractor lacks authentication; the other satisfies neither of the alternative granting conditions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 (p. 41); FL-4.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A session model has transitions Anonymous→SignedIn on login, SignedIn→Anonymous on logout and SignedIn→Expired on timeout. Tests login and logout only. What is state coverage?
questions.explanation: Anonymous and SignedIn are visited, but Expired is not. The denominator is the three modeled states, not the executed events; transition coverage is a different metric even where values coincide. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 (p. 41); FL-4.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Acceptance rules say cancellations before shipment return the full payment; cancellations after shipment are refused. Which example exposes an implementation that incorrectly refunds shipped orders?

options.text: Given Shipped, cancel; expect refusal and no refund
Given Shipped, cancel; expect a full refund
Given Unshipped, cancel; expect refusal
Given Unshipped, cancel; expect a full refund

questions.explanation: The correct case applies the negative rule to a shipped order. The valid unshipped case does not expose this defect; the other choices encode expectations contrary to the agreed rules. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Using a risk-rating model that multiplies likelihood by impact, what determines risk level?

options.text: Likelihood × impact
Requirement count × test count
Impact × number of developer comments
Likelihood × number of test scripts

questions.explanation: The stated model combines the chance rating and consequence rating. Script age, comment counts and IDs may be recorded but do not calculate risk level. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.1 (p. 52); FL-5.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A plan states the test approach but omits people and environments needed. What is the practical consequence?

options.text: Resource feasibility and responsibilities remain unclear
Every planned test automatically becomes invalid
The approach no longer describes any testing activity
The test results become available without execution

questions.explanation: Plans need resources and responsibilities to support delivery. Missing them creates uncertainty but does not automatically invalidate all cases or manufacture execution evidence. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.1 (p. 48); FL-5.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Automated component checks support developers while code is being built. Which quadrant fits their primary role?

options.text: Q3: business-facing critique
Q4: technology-facing critique
Q1: technology-facing support
Q2: business-facing support

questions.explanation: Component checks supporting development belong in Q1. Q2 uses business-facing guidance, while Q3 and Q4 primarily critique the product from their respective perspectives. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: A high-impact data-loss risk is identified. Which TWO responses can help address it?

options.text: Increase recovery testing and verify mitigation controls
Hide blocked recovery checks from the release report
Explicitly document residual risk for an informed acceptance decision
Assume the risk disappears after its first passing test

questions.explanation: Mitigation evidence and informed residual-risk acceptance are valid responses. One passing check cannot erase the risk, and concealing missing evidence prevents sound decisions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.4 (p. 53); FL-5.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: How does a test completion report primarily differ from a progress report?

options.text: It replaces detailed defect records with personal judgments
It consolidates milestone outcomes and remaining risk
It is only a list of future execution steps
It must contain no testing results

questions.explanation: Completion reporting consolidates achieved results, deviations and remaining risk. It can reference detailed findings but is not a future procedure or an appraisal of people. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.2 (p. 54); FL-5.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A release baseline is used for testing. What should it identify?

options.text: A promise that no later changes will occur
The agreed versions of related product and test items
An unordered collection of whatever files are newest
Only the date of the next team meeting

questions.explanation: A baseline provides an identifiable consistent set of versions. “Newest” without control is not reproducible, and dates or promises do not define configuration items. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team estimates 30 comparable cases remaining. Its observed execution rate is 6 cases per hour, with setup already complete. What is the extrapolated execution effort?

options.text: 24 hours
6 hours
5 hours
180 hours

questions.explanation: Effort is remaining cases divided by rate: 30/6=5 hours. Six repeats the rate, 24 subtracts quantities with different units, and 180 multiplies where division is needed. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Requirement priorities are R1 highest, R2 medium, R3 lowest. T1 checks R3, T2 checks R1 and T3 checks R2. There are no dependencies. Using requirements-based prioritization, what is the order?
questions.explanation: Order cases by their requirements’ priorities: the case for R1 is T2, then R2 is T3, then R3 is T1. Case numbers do not determine priority, and the absence of dependencies means the stated priority order can be applied directly. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: A reproducible issue loses customer data but the report calls it “cosmetic.” Which report field should be corrected to reflect observed consequences?

options.text: Reporter name
Submission timestamp
Severity
Test-case identifier

questions.explanation: Severity describes impact, so data loss is inconsistent with a cosmetic classification. Identity, reference and time fields do not communicate the seriousness of the failure. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team needs to organize cases, execution status and requirement coverage in one place. Which tool category is the best fit?

options.text: Static code analysis
Compiler optimization
Test management
Load generation

questions.explanation: Test-management tools support organizing and reporting testing evidence and links. Load tools exercise performance, analysis inspects code, and compiler optimization does not manage the test process. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO risks of test automation.

options.text: Incorrect oracles can give misleading passing results
Repeated routine work can require less manual effort
Flaky dependencies can reduce trust in feedback
Checks can execute consistently under controlled conditions

questions.explanation: Wrong expectations and flaky dependencies undermine useful evidence. Consistent execution and less repetitive manual work are potential benefits rather than the requested risks. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which activity is primarily quality assurance rather than product testing?

options.text: Measuring service response time under load
Reviewing a particular user story for contradictions
Improving the review process to prevent recurring omissions
Executing a checkout case and comparing the total

questions.explanation: Process improvement is QA-oriented prevention. Executing, measuring and reviewing specific work products are product evaluation activities, including static and dynamic testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.2 (p. 17); FL-1.2.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which behavior best supports shared quality responsibility?

options.text: Business representatives avoid clarifying examples
Collaborate on investigating failures and improving checks
Developers stop running checks once a tester joins
Testers conceal findings until the end of an iteration

questions.explanation: Joint investigation and improvement combine skills and support ownership. Abandoning checks, concealing evidence and avoiding clarification reduce the team's ability to address quality. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.2 (p. 22); FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A team finds that repeated requirement mistakes stem from excluding domain experts from refinement. What does that exclusion represent in this investigation?

options.text: A root cause
A runtime failure
The expected output of a test
An executable defect

questions.explanation: The exclusion is an underlying reason for recurring mistakes. It is not an observed runtime failure, code flaw or expected result; addressing it can help prevent repetition. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.3 (p. 17); FL-1.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A unchanged suite keeps passing, while recent incidents expose risks it never checked. Which response addresses tests wearing out?

options.text: Treat repeat passes as proof that incidents are unrelated
Refresh cases using evolving conditions
Rename existing passing cases without changing coverage
Remove the suite and stop regression testing

questions.explanation: Refreshing cases can reveal problems missed by unchanged checks. Renaming does not change evidence; passing old checks does not dismiss incidents, and useful regression still has value. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.3 (p. 17); FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A lead compares executed tests with the plan, then moves engineers to unblock high-risk cases. Which TWO activities are represented?

options.text: Test design
Test control
Test completion
Test monitoring

questions.explanation: Comparing actual progress with plans is monitoring; changing actions in response is control. The scenario does not derive new cases or consolidate a completed milestone. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.1 (p. 18); FL-1.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A project has a strict regulatory evidence requirement. How should that context affect its test process?

options.text: Remove documentation because execution is sufficient
Plan suitable traceability, records and review responsibilities
Treat tool selection as the sole compliance activity
Use the process from an unrelated informal prototype unchanged

questions.explanation: Context shapes evidence and responsibilities as well as execution. Copying an unsuitable approach, relying solely on tools or discarding records does not address the stated constraint. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.2 (p. 19); FL-1.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A defect is linked to its failing case, execution and original requirement. Which TWO uses do these links support?

options.text: Guaranteeing all other requirements pass
Automatically proving the root cause
Assessing which requirement is affected
Understanding the evidence behind the finding

questions.explanation: Links support impact and evidence assessment. They cannot by themselves diagnose causes or establish results for unrelated requirements. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.4 (p. 20); FL-1.4.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: A separate testing group finds defects but has little contact with developers and becomes a release bottleneck. What is the main drawback illustrated?

options.text: Developer checks are incompatible with independent testing
All testing must therefore be performed by authors
Organizational isolation can delay delivery
Independent perspectives cannot reveal new defects

questions.explanation: The issue is isolation and bottlenecking, a possible drawback of independence. Independent perspective can still be useful, and it can coexist with developer checks without forcing one universal staffing model. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.3 (p. 22); FL-1.5.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which good practice helps prevent downstream defects during development?

options.text: Wait for release packaging before considering testability
Assign every level an identical test basis
Involve testers in reviews of requirements and designs
Use production incidents as the first quality feedback

questions.explanation: Early tester involvement can expose ambiguity and testability problems. Waiting for packaging or incidents loses early feedback; test bases and objectives differ by level. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 25); FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which sequence best describes the core TDD cycle?

options.text: Write a failing test, make it pass, then refactor
Measure defect density, then choose a supplier
Refactor, deploy, then write an unexecuted test
Complete all features, then select acceptance participants

questions.explanation: TDD starts with a failing component test, adds sufficient implementation, and refactors with checks preserved. The other sequences concern unrelated or delayed activities rather than the cycle. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 26); FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: Tests are derived from source branches and assert the computed results. Which description is accurate?

options.text: They cannot check behavior because structure was used
They use white-box derivation and can still check functional behavior
They belong to acceptance level solely because assertions exist
They are static because the source was consulted

questions.explanation: A structural basis makes derivation white-box, but execution and assertions can assess behavior. Source knowledge does not make execution static or determine the test level. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.2 (p. 29); FL-2.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: An old service is being retired, with data retained for future audit. What maintenance-testing concern is appropriate?

options.text: Verify the archival and retrieval arrangements
Rerun an unrelated interface test without impact analysis
Test only features added to the retired service next year
Assume retirement makes retained data irrelevant

questions.explanation: Retirement can require verification of archival access and retention. Future features, ignoring data or choosing unrelated checks do not address the stated operational change. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.3 (p. 31); FL-2.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A sequential project maps planned acceptance testing to stakeholder needs and system testing to system requirements. What benefit does that mapping provide?

options.text: Proof that execution can find every possible defect
An obligation to use identical cases at all levels
A requirement for testing to avoid early reviews
A suitable test basis and objectives at each level

questions.explanation: Mapping levels to corresponding work products supports focused planning and evaluation. It does not promise exhaustiveness, prohibit reviews or make different levels interchangeable. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 25); FL-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO statements consistent with shift left.

options.text: Review requirements before defects propagate into code
Eliminate all system testing once component tests exist
Move every acceptance decision before stakeholder examples are agreed
Design relevant checks earlier while retaining later evaluation

questions.explanation: Earlier suitable activities provide feedback sooner, while later evaluation remains important. Shift left neither eliminates system testing nor bypasses agreement on stakeholder expectations. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.5 (p. 27); FL-2.1.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: Frequent feedback on small increments most directly helps a team do what?

options.text: Replace confirmation testing after defect fixes
Adjust understanding when stakeholder needs change
Guarantee that the original requirements never evolve
Avoid communicating about completed behavior

questions.explanation: Frequent feedback helps detect changed or misunderstood needs. It does not freeze requirements, remove communication or provide confirmation of a code fix by itself. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.1 (p. 35); FL-3.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which review practice supports a constructive culture?

options.text: Reward reviewers for agreeing regardless of evidence
Use findings to rank individual authors publicly
Discuss defects in the work product using clear evidence
Prevent clarification questions to shorten the meeting

questions.explanation: Focusing on work-product evidence supports useful evaluation. Public ranking, pressured agreement and suppressed clarification undermine review goals and psychological safety. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.5 (p. 37); FL-3.2.5 (K1).

questions.prompt: A static analysis tool flags unreachable code before execution. What benefit can this provide?

options.text: Measured evidence of peak-load response time
Early detection of flaws in source structure
A guarantee that every flagged issue is a user-visible failure
Replacement of requirements-based testing

questions.explanation: Static analysis can detect structural issues before dynamic testing. It does not measure runtime load, guarantee user-visible consequences for every finding or replace requirements evidence. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.2 (p. 33); FL-3.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team chooses the most formal review type, with defined roles, prescribed steps and collected review information. Which type best fits?

options.text: Author-led walkthrough
Inspection
Informal review
Exploratory session

questions.explanation: Inspection is the most formal review type. Informal reviews have fewer prescribed steps, walkthroughs are typically author-led, and exploratory sessions execute and investigate software rather than review an artifact this way. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.4 (p. 36); FL-3.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why combine specification-based and structure-based techniques?

options.text: They ensure each technique finds identical defects
They make experience-based investigation unusable
They expose different coverage gaps
They remove the need for expected outcomes
