questions.explanation: Requirements coverage and structural reachability address different omissions. Combining them broadens evidence without guaranteeing identical findings, removing oracles or excluding experience-based work. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.1 (p. 39); FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A suite reports 80% statement coverage. Which interpretation is justified?

options.text: Exactly 20% of decision outcomes were not taken
Exactly 20% of the product's defects remain
Some executable statements were not exercised
Exactly 20% of requirements are missing

questions.explanation: Statement coverage describes executed statements. It cannot be converted directly into requirements, branches or defect percentages; those need their own evidence. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 (p. 42); FL-4.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO accurate statements about branch coverage.

options.text: Full statement coverage necessarily includes full branch coverage
It measures exercised control-flow branches
Full branch coverage includes full statement coverage for the modeled structure
It measures the percentage of requirements accepted by users

questions.explanation: Branches concern control-flow choices, and covering all modeled branches also reaches their statements. The reverse implication fails; requirements acceptance is a different measure. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 (p. 43); FL-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester anticipates an off-by-one error after studying a team's recurring mistakes and adds a targeted case. What is the main technique?

options.text: Error-based execution scheduling
Formal review inspection
Error guessing
Configuration baselining

questions.explanation: A plausible fault based on experience motivates error guessing. Scheduling and baselining organize work and versions; inspection reviews a work product rather than derives this runtime case. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 (p. 43); FL-4.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: During exploratory testing, an unexpected save behavior is observed. What is an appropriate next step?

options.text: Declare complete coverage from the first session
Design a focused experiment and record what it reveals
Replace all observations with a count of button presses
Ignore it because it was absent from the initial charter

questions.explanation: Exploration adapts to observations while retaining evidence. Ignoring discoveries, overclaiming coverage or recording only clicks prevents useful learning and communication. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 (p. 44); FL-4.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Criterion: “The screen should feel nice.” What is its main weakness as acceptance criteria?

options.text: It requires a specific implementation algorithm
It specifies a test framework too precisely
It contains too many measurable thresholds
It lacks an agreed observable basis for evaluation

questions.explanation: The phrase gives no shared observable expectation. The problem is ambiguity, rather than excessive detail or prescribed tools and implementation. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 (p. 45); FL-4.5.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A shipping result has four output partitions: domestic free, domestic paid, international paid and rejected address. Existing cases produce both domestic outputs and a rejected address. Which additional case closes the output-partition gap?

options.text: An international address producing rejection
An international address producing paid delivery
A domestic address producing free delivery
A domestic address producing paid delivery

questions.explanation: The suite has exercised three of the four specified output classes. An international paid-delivery outcome covers the remaining class. More examples of the already covered outputs do not close this partition gap. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: Integer scores have partitions below 50, 50–79 and 80 or above. Which set covers two-value BVA at both boundaries?
questions.explanation: The adjacent cross-partition pairs are 49/50 and 79/80. Other sets skip a boundary or the closest value across it, so they do not provide the requested boundary coverage. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A fee table has two Boolean conditions, Premium and Express. Premium=false with Express=true is infeasible. How many feasible rules remain in the full decision table?
questions.explanation: Two Boolean conditions initially give four combinations. Excluding the one stated infeasible combination leaves three. Two counts too few, four fails to exclude it, and eight introduces another condition. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 (p. 41); FL-4.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: From Ready, send moves to Waiting; from Waiting, reply moves to Done. Cancel is invalid in Waiting and must leave the state unchanged. Which test correctly checks the invalid transition?

options.text: Send, then cancel; expect state Done
Start Ready, then cancel; expect state Waiting
Send, then cancel; expect rejection and state Waiting
Send, then inspect; expect the initial state Ready

questions.explanation: Cancel from Waiting is explicitly invalid, so rejection with unchanged state is the correct expectation. The other tests cover valid behavior or states without attempting an invalid event. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 (p. 41); FL-4.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Criterion: only active members can reserve; an active member cannot have more than two concurrent reservations. Which case tests the count restriction independently of membership eligibility?

options.text: Active member with no reservations adds one; expect refusal
Inactive member with two reservations adds one; expect success
Active member with two reservations adds one; expect refusal
Inactive member with no reservations adds one; expect refusal

questions.explanation: An eligible active member already at the limit isolates the count restriction. Inactive cases involve membership, and refusing the eligible empty account or accepting an inactive one contradicts the rules. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Which is a metric useful for monitoring test progress?

options.text: Number of characters in the project name
Alphabetical rank of the test leader
Number of unused meeting rooms
Number of planned tests executed

questions.explanation: Executed tests compared with the plan can indicate progress, though results and risk context are also needed. Naming and unrelated administrative quantities do not measure test progress. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.1 (p. 54); FL-5.3.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A completion criterion is unmet, but stakeholders consider releasing anyway. What is an appropriate response?

options.text: Delete evidence of the incomplete testing
Claim testing achieved its original objective unchanged
Report the deviation and residual risk for an explicit decision
Redefine the criterion silently to match current results

questions.explanation: Criteria support decisions rather than conceal uncertainty. Explicitly reporting deviations and risks permits an informed exception; silent changes and erased evidence misrepresent outcomes. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.3 (p. 49); FL-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: An agreed business-facing acceptance example guides implementation of a discount. Which quadrant best fits?

options.text: Q4: technology-facing product critique
Q1: technology-facing support for development
Q3: business-facing product critique
Q2: business-facing support for development

questions.explanation: The example guides work using business expectations, the purpose of Q2. Q1 concerns technical support, and Q3/Q4 primarily evaluate the finished product from different perspectives. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: A supplier cannot deliver the test environment on schedule, while the product may leak confidential data. How are these risks classified?

options.text: Both are project because a deadline exists
Both are product because testing is involved
Environment delay is project; data leakage is product
Environment delay is product; data leakage is project

questions.explanation: The delay threatens project delivery; leakage threatens product quality. Context does not collapse these different consequences into one category. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.2 (p. 52); FL-5.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A dashboard shows 95% of executed tests passed but omits blocked security tests. What should a status update add?

options.text: A claim that the displayed pass percentage establishes readiness
The same percentage with more decimal places
The coverage gap and its implications for release risk
Names of people assigned to the blocked cases

questions.explanation: The missing high-risk evidence changes interpretation of the pass percentage. Precision or ownership alone is insufficient; the gap and decision implications must be communicated. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.3 (p. 55); FL-5.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO items that should be controlled for reproducible testing.

options.text: An unrelated application's popularity rating
The tester's lunch choice
The test-data version
The environment configuration

questions.explanation: Data and environment changes can alter observations, so their configuration belongs in reproducible evidence. Personal preferences and unrelated ratings do not define the test conditions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: For a three-point estimate, use standard deviation SD=(P−O)/6. Optimistic effort is 6 days and pessimistic effort is 18 days. What is SD?

options.text: 3 days
2 days
6 days
12 days

questions.explanation: Substitute the bounds into the specified uncertainty formula: (18−6)/6=12/6=2 days. Twelve is the range before division; six is the optimistic input; neither is the standard deviation. This measure describes estimation uncertainty, not the expected effort. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: T1 covers A,B; T2 covers A,B,C,D; T3 covers E,F,G. No dependencies apply. Use coverage-based prioritization by total items covered, without recalculating additional coverage. What is the order?
questions.explanation: Total coverage counts are four for T2, three for T3 and two for T1. Descending totals give T2,T3,T1. The question explicitly asks for total coverage, so overlapping items are not removed after selecting a test. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: A reproducible data-loss issue has severe impact, but a documented workaround permits the release owner to schedule its fix later. Which report classification reflects impact separately from agreed urgency?

options.text: Low severity because the fix is scheduled later
Omit impact because a workaround has been approved
High severity with lower fix priority
High urgency solely because the title sounds serious

questions.explanation: Severity records the serious consequence of data loss; priority records the agreed urgency of remediation. A workaround can affect scheduling without making the underlying impact low. A title cannot establish urgency, and impact should remain documented. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: An unavailable payment gateway blocks tests. A tool supplies configurable responses in its place. What support is being used?

options.text: Defect trend reporting
Static analysis
Statement coverage measurement
Service virtualization

questions.explanation: Virtualization substitutes controlled behavior for a dependency. Static analysis inspects artifacts, coverage measures executed structure, and trends summarize findings rather than simulate the gateway. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why run a pilot before adopting an automation tool widely?

options.text: Avoid involving the people who will maintain checks
Conclude that manual activities should be automated
Evaluate integration, maintenance and useful feedback in context
Certify maintenance-free scripts for later versions

questions.explanation: A pilot supplies evidence about fit, costs and value. It cannot guarantee maintenance-free scripts, and excluding maintainers or assuming universal automation undermines the evaluation. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which purpose is a typical reason for evaluating software work products?

options.text: Negotiating a hosting contract
Scheduling a sales campaign
Supporting a release decision
Assigning a developer bonus

questions.explanation: Testing supplies quality and risk evidence for decisions. Personnel rewards, hosting negotiations and marketing schedules are not typical test objectives. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.1 (p. 15); FL-1.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: An engineer locates a memory leak and changes allocation logic. Which activity does this describe?

options.text: Debugging the implementation
Designing test conditions
Monitoring the schedule
Reviewing acceptance criteria

questions.explanation: Locating and repairing a cause is debugging. Case design, progress tracking and criteria review do not perform the repair described. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.2 (p. 16); FL-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A review exposes conflicting billing rules before implementation begins. How does this help?

options.text: It fixes a deployed incident
It reduces avoidable rework
It measures peak throughput
It computes branch coverage

questions.explanation: Resolving conflicting rules early can prevent downstream defects and rework. Review does not measure runtime load or executed branches; the feature has not been deployed. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.1 (p. 16); FL-1.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between testing and quality assurance?

options.text: Testing recruits reviewers; QA derives boundaries
Testing evaluates products; QA improves processes
Testing prices deliveries; QA approves invoices
Testing allocates budgets; QA measures latency

questions.explanation: Testing contributes product-oriented quality control; QA focuses on processes producing and evaluating work. The other pairings assign unrelated duties or confuse the concerns. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.2 (p. 17); FL-1.2.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Missing training leads an analyst to misunderstand a rule, write a faulty requirement, and cause incorrect charges when implemented. What is the faulty requirement?

options.text: A root cause in staff training
A defect in a work product
A failure observed by a user
An error made by the analyst

questions.explanation: The incorrect requirement is a defect. Misunderstanding is the error; missing training is a candidate root cause; observed wrong charges are failures. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.3 (p. 17); FL-1.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team adds new cases for newly introduced offline operation while retaining useful regression checks. Which principle explains this need?

options.text: Defects cluster in historically faulty areas
Exhaustive testing has a fixed duration
Context fixes the same number of cases
Tests lose effectiveness as risks evolve

questions.explanation: Repeated checks need review as new behavior and risks emerge. Clustering concerns concentrations of defects; the other options misstate exhaustiveness and context. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.3 (p. 17); FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester prepares scripts, orders procedures and configures data for an upcoming run. Which activity is described?

options.text: Test completion
Test implementation
Test analysis
Test monitoring

questions.explanation: Implementation prepares procedures, suites, data and environments. Analysis identifies what to test; monitoring assesses progress; completion consolidates milestone evidence. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.1 (p. 18); FL-1.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A prototype and a safety-critical controller have different consequences of failure. How should this affect their evaluation?

options.text: Prioritize the one with fewer end users
Adapt scope to their respective risks
Set equal effort using their line counts
Apply the same cases to both products

questions.explanation: Context, including consequences and risk, influences the approach. Line counts, shared code use and user counts alone cannot establish suitable scope or rigor. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.2 (p. 19); FL-1.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which work product results from turning conditions into detailed checks?

options.text: Logs with observed outcomes
Reports with residual risks
Directives with revised schedules
Cases with expected outcomes

questions.explanation: Design develops cases, inputs and expected results. Logs are execution outputs; residual-risk reports consolidate results; schedule directives are control outputs. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.3 (p. 20); FL-1.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A business rule changes and linked cases are identified immediately. What benefit is illustrated?

options.text: Environment provisioning
Impact assessment
Runtime load measurement
Automatic defect repair

questions.explanation: Traceability identifies affected testware when the basis changes. It does not itself measure load, repair the implementation or provision an environment. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.4 (p. 20); FL-1.4.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: One person coordinates staffing and another derives cases from requirements. Which pair of responsibilities fits?

options.text: Scribe role and reviewer role
Supplier role and customer role
Management role and testing role
Author role and moderator role

questions.explanation: Coordination fits test management; technical analysis and design fit the testing role. Review and commercial roles do not describe this division. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.5 (p. 21); FL-1.4.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: A report gives reproducible steps and separates observations from blame. Which skill is demonstrated?

options.text: Statistical load generation
Constructive communication
Memory-allocation programming
Contract-price negotiation

questions.explanation: Clear factual communication makes findings usable and supports collaboration. The scenario does not demonstrate programming, commercial or performance-tool expertise. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.1 (p. 21); FL-1.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: In the whole-team approach, which responsibility is shared?

options.text: Custody of the corporate trademark
Quality of the delivered product
Administration of the payroll system
Authorization of supplier payments

questions.explanation: The team shares quality responsibility and brings complementary skills. This approach does not assign unrelated administrative or legal duties. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.2 (p. 22); FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A separate group finds assumptions developers missed but struggles to obtain domain clarification. What does this illustrate?

options.text: Identical biases with reduced reporting effort
Shared implementation with easier data access
Different perspectives with a collaboration cost
Lower independence with faster diagnosis

questions.explanation: Independent perspectives can expose assumptions, while separation can impede communication. The other descriptions contradict the stated separation and clarification difficulty. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.3 (p. 22); FL-1.5.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team replaces a single large delivery with usable increments each fortnight. Which adjustment is appropriate?

options.text: Keep the original large-delivery schedule without revision
Check new and affected existing behavior in each increment
Defer product evaluation until the final increment arrives
Replace requirement review with one deployment approval

questions.explanation: Frequent increments need fast feedback and regression evidence alongside new-feature checks. Deferring evaluation or keeping an unadapted schedule misses the changed lifecycle. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 25); FL-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which practice applies across development lifecycles?

options.text: Replace planning with a final status report
Review drafts as they become available
Start case design after deployment
Give each level the same objective

questions.explanation: Early review of available work products is a lifecycle-independent good practice. Late design, identical objectives and replacing planning weaken evaluation. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 25); FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which sequence characterizes test-driven development?

options.text: Prepare a manual, run training, then review results
Write a test, implement enough code, then refactor
Implement a feature, deploy it, then draft its tests
Approve release, archive findings, then rewrite code

questions.explanation: TDD uses tests to guide implementation and refactoring. The other sequences lack the test-first development loop. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 26); FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: An organization integrates development and operations around frequent delivery. Which cost belongs in its plan?

options.text: Maintaining the pipeline and its checks
Removing representative data preparation
Replacing exploration with deployment logs
Avoiding integration between toolchains

questions.explanation: DevOps requires maintained delivery tools and automation resources. Data, human exploration and tool integration still require effort despite automated feedback. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.4 (p. 26); FL-2.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which action most clearly moves evaluation earlier?

options.text: Updating a completion report at retirement
Reviewing a draft interface contract
Repeating a case after a production fix
Archiving results after release approval

questions.explanation: Draft review can reveal defects before implementation. The other actions occur after production repair, release or retirement. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.5 (p. 27); FL-2.1.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team agrees to improve fixture provisioning in its retrospective. What completes the improvement loop?

options.text: Replace the next backlog with meeting minutes
Check the effect in subsequent iterations
Record attendees in the project directory
Defer ownership until another incident

questions.explanation: An improvement needs implementation and evaluation of its effects. Administrative records, deferred ownership and substituting minutes for work do not demonstrate improvement. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.6 (p. 28); FL-2.1.6 (K2).

questions.prompt: A check exercises message exchange between a shop and an external bank. Which level describes this scope?

options.text: Component isolation testing
Component integration testing
Business acceptance testing
System integration testing

questions.explanation: Interfaces with external systems are system integration concerns. Internal units and their interactions have smaller scope; acceptance has stakeholder-readiness objectives. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.1 (p. 28); FL-2.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A check measures how quickly a report is produced under concurrent use. Which type describes its focus?

options.text: Confirmation testing
Functional rule testing
Static document review
Non-functional testing

questions.explanation: Response time under load is non-functional. There is no repaired defect or review described; the focus is performance rather than calculation rules. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.2 (p. 29); FL-2.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: After an address fix, the team repeats the original failure case and checks related delivery calculations. What are the respective purposes?

options.text: Static analysis and inspection
Monitoring and completion
Confirmation and regression
Acceptance and maintenance

questions.explanation: Repeating the failing case checks the repair; related calculations check adverse effects. The alternatives are other activities or contexts rather than these purposes. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.3 (p. 30); FL-2.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: An operational service moves to another storage provider. Which approach is appropriate?

options.text: Adopt old-provider results as the new baseline
Assess affected access, data and interfaces
Limit scope to edited application lines
Treat unchanged source as sufficient evidence

questions.explanation: Migration can alter data, interfaces and runtime behavior without source changes. Impact analysis guides maintenance scope; old results concern the previous configuration. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.3 (p. 31); FL-2.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which work product can be reviewed before executable software exists?

options.text: A draft API contract
A measured peak throughput
A recorded runtime heap size
A live request completion time

questions.explanation: A contract can be inspected for omissions and contradictions. Throughput, heap use and completion time are runtime observations requiring execution. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.1 (p. 33); FL-3.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A review finds conflicting eligibility rules. What is a direct benefit of resolving the finding?

options.text: Estimating observed transaction latency
Preventing downstream implementation defects
Measuring production resource consumption
Increasing executed branch coverage

questions.explanation: Early static findings can prevent propagation and rework. Review does not measure runtime consumption, reached branches or observed latency. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.2 (p. 33); FL-3.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly distinguishes review evidence from execution evidence?

options.text: A contradiction and a timeout
A live latency and a role assignment
A runtime leak and an inspection plan
A peak throughput and a contract revision

questions.explanation: Review can reveal a contradiction directly; execution can reveal a timeout. The other pairs assign runtime measurements to review or administrative changes to execution. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.3 (p. 34); FL-3.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: What benefit comes from early, frequent stakeholder feedback on drafts?

options.text: Computing executed code coverage in advance
Replacing environment setup with meeting notes
Detecting misunderstood needs sooner
Repairing runtime memory allocation directly

questions.explanation: Frequent feedback supports shared understanding and clarification. It does not directly repair runtime code, measure unexecuted coverage or substitute for environments. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.1 (p. 35); FL-3.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Participants examine a document separately and record candidate anomalies ahead of the discussion. Which activity is described?

options.text: Review initiation
Fixing and reporting
Communication and analysis
Individual review

questions.explanation: Individual review produces candidate findings. Initiation prepares participation; communication analyzes findings together; fixing and reporting follow agreed actions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.2 (p. 35); FL-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Who records agreed findings during a formal review?

options.text: The author
The manager
The moderator
The scribe

questions.explanation: The scribe records findings and decisions. The author updates the work, management supports resources and the moderator facilitates discussion. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.3 (p. 36); FL-3.2.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: A review uses defined roles, preparation and metrics for process improvement. Which type is the most formal?

options.text: Inspection
Walkthrough
Informal review
Exploratory session

questions.explanation: Inspection is the most formal review type. Walkthroughs are generally author-led; informal reviews have less prescribed structure; exploration is a dynamic technique. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.4 (p. 36); FL-3.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which arrangement supports a useful review?

options.text: Manageable scope with preparation time
Large scope with immediate discussion
Public rankings of individual authors
Undocumented findings with rapid approval

questions.explanation: Manageable work and preparation support examination. Excessive scope, personal ranking and missing evidence impair useful findings and constructive participation. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.5 (p. 37); FL-3.2.5 (K1).

questions.prompt: Cases are derived from specified behavior rather than internal decisions. Which family is used?

options.text: Experience-based techniques
Configuration-management techniques
Black-box techniques
White-box techniques

questions.explanation: Specification-derived cases are black-box. Structural derivation is white-box; knowledge of likely faults motivates experience-based work. Configuration management controls versions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.1 (p. 39); FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Integer quantity is rejected below 3, accepted from 3 through 8, and rejected above 8. Which set covers these three partitions?
questions.explanation: 2 covers the lower invalid group, 5 the valid group and 9 the upper invalid group. Each other set misses at least one identified partition. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: An integer score is valid from 20 through 24. Which set achieves full two-value BVA across both partition edges?
questions.explanation: Adjacent cross-partition pairs are 19/20 and 24/25. The alternatives omit boundaries or their immediate neighbors across an edge. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A decision table has eight feasible rules and six have been exercised. What rule coverage has been achieved?
questions.explanation: Coverage is exercised feasible rules divided by total feasible rules: 6/8=75%. Conditions and possible input values are not the denominator. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 (p. 41); FL-4.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Draft --submit--> Pending; Pending --reject--> Draft; Pending --approve--> Approved. Which sequence from Draft covers all three valid transitions?

options.text: submit, reject, submit, reject
submit, submit, reject, approve
submit, reject, submit, approve
submit, approve, reject, submit

questions.explanation: The key follows each stated transition and reaches Approved last. Reject from Approved and submit from Pending are not stated transitions; repeated rejection misses approval. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 (p. 41); FL-4.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A suite executes nine of twelve executable statements. What does the resulting 75% describe?

options.text: Requirements coverage
Defect detection percentage
Decision-rule coverage
Statement coverage

questions.explanation: Nine divided by twelve measures executed statements. Requirements, defects and decision rules are different items with different denominators. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 (p. 42); FL-4.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A suite exercises every branch in the executable structure. Which statement is justified?

options.text: It also detects the complete defect population
It also exercises each possible path combination
It also reaches full statement coverage
It also verifies the complete requirement set

questions.explanation: Branch coverage subsumes statement coverage. It does not establish requirements completeness, removal of defects or all combinations of paths. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 (p. 43); FL-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A required export format is absent from the implementation. Why can structural coverage miss this omission?

options.text: It measures the code that exists
It measures stakeholder satisfaction
It measures deployed business value
It measures documented acceptance scope

questions.explanation: Structural metrics count implementation items; nonexistent required behavior provides no code item to reach. Specification-derived checks address omissions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 (p. 43); FL-4.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester recalls failures caused by empty filenames and creates related checks. Which technique is illustrated?

options.text: State-model traversal
Error guessing
Decision-table derivation
Branch-based derivation

questions.explanation: The checks arise from experience of likely faults. The other methods require rule combinations, structure or a state model, none of which is the stated basis. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 (p. 43); FL-4.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: In a chartered session, an unexpected response guides the next investigation. Which description fits?

options.text: Design ends before the initial observation
The charter determines each click in advance
Session notes substitute for actual execution
Learning, design and execution evolve together

questions.explanation: Exploratory work adapts further design and execution to observations. It retains a mission and evidence without prescribing every action beforehand. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 (p. 44); FL-4.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A reusable list reminds testers to check interruption, persistence and messages while allowing cases to vary. Which technique fits?

options.text: Decision-table testing
Boundary-value testing
Checklist-based testing
Statement-based testing

questions.explanation: A list of conditions guides checklist-based work. Statements, condition combinations and ordered boundaries are other derivation bases. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 (p. 44); FL-4.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Business staff, a developer and a tester discuss concrete examples for a story. What is the main benefit?

options.text: Shared understanding of desired behavior
Replacement of the operational environment
Automatic structural-coverage calculation
Transfer of the release budget to the team

questions.explanation: Collaboration clarifies the story through complementary perspectives. It does not supply runtime resources, measure code coverage or transfer budget ownership. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 (p. 45); FL-4.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Acceptance criteria list constraints as a checklist rather than Given/When/Then examples. Which style is used?

options.text: Rule-oriented criteria
Scenario-oriented criteria
Implementation branch criteria
Review participation criteria

questions.explanation: Constraints listed as rules are rule-oriented. Scenario-oriented criteria describe situations and outcomes; branch and participation criteria concern other processes. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 (p. 45); FL-4.5.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A ticket is refundable when unused and requested at least 48 hours before departure. Which case isolates rejection for prior use?

options.text: Used ticket, requested 30 hours before departure
Unused ticket, requested 60 hours before departure
Used ticket, requested 60 hours before departure
Unused ticket, requested 47 hours before departure

questions.explanation: Used/60 satisfies time and violates usage alone. Unused/47 isolates time, used/30 violates both and unused/60 is accepted. Isolate rules to make failures interpretable. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Which work product communicates scope, responsibilities, environment needs and completion criteria?

options.text: Test plan
Execution log
Defect report
Coverage trace

questions.explanation: A test plan coordinates objectives, approach and resources. Logs record runs, defect reports describe anomalies and traces link evidence to the basis. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.1 (p. 48); FL-5.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which contribution is appropriate for a tester during iteration planning?

options.text: Set external supplier trademark policy
Identify checks and estimate their effort
Approve annual payroll adjustments
Negotiate enterprise office rental

questions.explanation: Testers refine testability, risks, tasks and effort. The alternatives are unrelated administrative or commercial responsibilities. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.2 (p. 48); FL-5.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: The deadline arrives while important checks remain blocked. What supports an informed completion decision?

options.text: Remove the blocked requirements silently
Substitute historical runs for remaining results
Report unmet criteria and residual risks
Reclassify blocked checks as passed cases

questions.explanation: Decisions need deviations and remaining risk. Changing outcomes, removing scope without disclosure and substituting past evidence misrepresent the current evaluation. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.3 (p. 49); FL-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Using E=(O+4M+P)/6 with O=3, M=6 and P=15 days, what is expected effort?

options.text: 7 days
6 days
8 days
12 days

questions.explanation: E=(3+24+15)/6=7 days. Six is the most likely input; eight is the unweighted average; twelve is the range rather than expected effort. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: T1 covers P,Q; T2 covers Q,R,S; T3 covers T,U. T2 is selected. Which remaining test supplies more additional coverage?

options.text: T1 adds two items
T3 adds one item
T1 adds three items
T3 adds two items

questions.explanation: After T2, T1 adds P and T3 adds T,U. Additional coverage excludes already-covered items; total size alone is not the criterion. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: Which distribution reflects the general test-pyramid model?

options.text: One broad check replacing lower-layer checks
Many small isolated checks and fewer broad checks
Many broad UI checks and fewer isolated checks
Equal counts at each layer regardless of cost

questions.explanation: The pyramid favors many fast isolated checks and fewer slower broad checks. Layer names vary; it does not require equal counts or replacement of lower levels. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.6 (p. 50); FL-5.1.6 (K1).

questions.prompt: A session evaluates how real users accomplish tasks with the finished product. Which quadrant fits this business focus and critical purpose?

options.text: Q3
Q1
Q2
Q4

questions.explanation: Q3 is business-facing and critiques the product. Q2 guides development with business examples; Q1 and Q4 are technology-facing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which attributes define the assessment of risk level?

options.text: Statement count and branch count
Reporter tenure and team size
Likelihood and impact
Case count and build size

questions.explanation: Risk level reflects chance of an adverse event and its consequences. Test, code and staff counts are not the defining pair. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.1 (p. 52); FL-5.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A specialist leaves, delaying evaluation. Incorrect tax in delivered invoices threatens customers. What are these risks respectively?

options.text: Project risk and product risk
Product risk and project risk
Two configuration risks of the same type
Two review findings rather than risks

questions.explanation: Staff loss threatens schedule, a project concern. Wrong delivered calculations threaten product quality. Related events can still have different risk categories. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.2 (p. 52); FL-5.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Assessment ranks settlement errors above cosmetic issues. Which consequence is appropriate?

options.text: Defer financial checks until cosmetic work completes
Allocate deeper checks to the financial rules
Allocate effort according to screen pixel counts
Use equal scope for each item regardless of harm

questions.explanation: Risk analysis affects scope, thoroughness and priority. Pixel counts, indiscriminate equal scope and delaying higher-risk work do not follow this assessment. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.3 (p. 52); FL-5.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team adds security checks and then evaluates effectiveness and emerging exposure. Which activities are described?

options.text: Risk mitigation and risk monitoring
Risk identification and staff recruitment
Risk transfer and document archiving
Risk acceptance and schedule cancellation

questions.explanation: Implementing measures mitigates risk; evaluating effectiveness and new exposure monitors risk. The other pairs do not describe these actions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.4 (p. 53); FL-5.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which quantity is a test-progress metric?

options.text: Number of competing product trademarks
Number of planned cases executed
Number of corporate office locations
Number of customer invoice addresses

questions.explanation: Executed cases against the plan describe progress. Administrative and commercial counts do not describe the activity; progress still needs outcomes and risk context. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.1 (p. 54); FL-5.3.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A cycle has ended and stakeholders need achieved objectives, deviations and unresolved issues. Which report fits?

options.text: Environment access request
Test completion report
Daily test progress report
Individual review finding

questions.explanation: Completion reporting consolidates an activity for later decisions. Progress reports support ongoing control; findings and requests have narrower purposes. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.2 (p. 54); FL-5.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A sponsor receives a 95% completion figure while unexecuted cases concern deletion of personal data. What additional information matters most?

options.text: Untested scope and its release implications
Sorting order of executed case titles
Average length of completed case names
Author count in the archived case directory

questions.explanation: Stakeholders need the significance of the remaining scope and risks. Presentation statistics and directory counts do not explain the decision implications. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.3 (p. 55); FL-5.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Two runs differ after a fixture update. Which record best supports investigation?

options.text: Office location and email signature for each run
Build, case and data revisions for each run
Tester preference and editor theme for each run
Meeting attendance and room number for each run

questions.explanation: Versioned product, cases and data identify configurations behind observations. Personal and administrative details cannot establish why results changed. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A report asserts “the wrong variable caused it” without supporting investigation. Which revision makes the observation actionable?

options.text: Record the suspected variable and omit observed amounts
Record the developer name and request personal discipline
Record a release date and attach an unrelated screenshot
Record inputs, expected amount, actual amount and evidence

questions.explanation: Reproduction conditions, expected and actual outcomes and evidence support triage. Unsupported diagnosis, blame and unrelated attachments impede it; mark suspected causes as hypotheses. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tool flags unreachable code without running the application. Which category fits?

options.text: Static analysis support
Load generation support
Runtime comparison support
Deployment rollback support

questions.explanation: Static analysis inspects structured work products without executing the object. The alternatives concern workload, runtime observations or deployment actions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

options.text: Elimination of environment configuration effort

questions.explanation: Automation can improve consistency and reduce repetition. Expected results, human investigation and maintained environments still require work and judgment. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).
